topics.name: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 1 - Embedded Systems and ARM Architectures: Review of embedded systems fundamentals from DESN2000. Introduction to ARM Cortex-A9 (ARMv7) and Cortex-A53 (ARMv8) architectures. Overview of memory maps, boot sequences, exception processing, and interrupt handling, as required for bare-metal code implementation in Lab 1. Introduction to embedded C programming. Discussion of the role of embedded systems in modern digital platforms.
topics.description: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 1 - Embedded Systems and ARM Architectures: Review of embedded systems fundamentals from DESN2000. Introduction to ARM Cortex-A9 (ARMv7) and Cortex-A53 (ARMv8) architectures. Overview of memory maps, boot sequences, exception processing, and interrupt handling, as required for bare-metal code implementation in Lab 1. Introduction to embedded C programming. Discussion of the role of embedded systems in modern digital platforms. in Digital and Embedded Systems Design.

topics.name: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 2 - Digital Logic Design with Verilog: Review of digital logic concepts from ELEC2141. Introduction to Verilog HDL for combinational and sequential logic design. Design and simulation of multiplexers, flip-flops, counters, and registers. Finite State Machines (FSMs): Mealy and Moore models, state diagrams, transition tables, and state minimisation techniques. Lab 2 will focus on Moore-style FSM design.
topics.description: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 2 - Digital Logic Design with Verilog: Review of digital logic concepts from ELEC2141. Introduction to Verilog HDL for combinational and sequential logic design. Design and simulation of multiplexers, flip-flops, counters, and registers. Finite State Machines (FSMs): Mealy and Moore models, state diagrams, transition tables, and state minimisation techniques. Lab 2 will focus on Moore-style FSM design. in Digital and Embedded Systems Design.

topics.name: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 3 - Programmable Logic Devices and FPGA Architecture: Overview of PLA, PAL, CPLD, and FPGA technologies. FPGA design flow: RTL design, synthesis, placement, routing, and bitstream generation. Internal FPGA architecture, including Configurable Logic Blocks (CLBs), Slices, and Block RAM (BRAM). Introduction to the Xilinx Vivado Design Suite and basic hardware debugging concepts. Vivado’s built-in logic analyser (ILA) will be used in Lab 3 for debugging real hardware behaviour.
topics.description: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 3 - Programmable Logic Devices and FPGA Architecture: Overview of PLA, PAL, CPLD, and FPGA technologies. FPGA design flow: RTL design, synthesis, placement, routing, and bitstream generation. Internal FPGA architecture, including Configurable Logic Blocks (CLBs), Slices, and Block RAM (BRAM). Introduction to the Xilinx Vivado Design Suite and basic hardware debugging concepts. Vivado’s built-in logic analyser (ILA) will be used in Lab 3 for debugging real hardware behaviour. in Digital and Embedded Systems Design.

topics.name: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 4 - Interfacing and Communication Protocols: Introduction to digital interfacing concepts from DESN2000 and ELEC2117. Overview of data/address buses, I2C, UART, and CAN protocols. In-depth study of bus architecture with focus on AXI4, AXI-Lite, and AXI-Stream protocols. PS-PL interfacing in Zynq SoCs. Logic families and voltage level compatibility.
topics.description: 2 Lectures of 2+1 (3) hours and 1 Tutorial of 2 hours. Lecture 4 - Interfacing and Communication Protocols: Introduction to digital interfacing concepts from DESN2000 and ELEC2117. Overview of data/address buses, I2C, UART, and CAN protocols. In-depth study of bus architecture with focus on AXI4, AXI-Lite, and AXI-Stream protocols. PS-PL interfacing in Zynq SoCs. topics.name: Week 1 core material covers: Course Introduction; What is Data Visualisation; Introduction to basic data visualisation theory including an introduction to Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics and an introduction to Constructing Charts in R using ggplot2. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will have personal introductions plus an (optional) one minute presentation of your favourite data visualsiation ). We will then do a brief introduction to R and RStudio; an introduction to git version control, and then do some hands-on data visualisation using ggplot2, exploring a range of chart types.
topics.description: Week 1 core material covers: Course Introduction; What is Data Visualisation; Introduction to basic data visualisation theory including an introduction to Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics and an introduction to Constructing Charts in R using ggplot2. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will have personal introductions plus an (optional) one minute presentation of your favourite data visualsiation ). We will then do a brief introduction to R and RStudio; an introduction to git version control, and then do some hands-on data visualisation using ggplot2, exploring a range of chart types. in Visualisation and Communication of Health Data.

topics.name: Week 2 core material covers an introduction to Literate Programming for scientific communication and some further examination of visualisation theory and best practices. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will look at communication by self-publishing, with a hands-on exercise of setting up your own health data science blog (which you can keep using after the course) and populating it with some initial content including an example visualisation.

topics.name: Week 3 core material covers a range of foundational topics and knowledge which are essential underpinnings to data visualisation tasks (and many other data science tasks besides): dplyr and the R tidyverse for data manipulation; fundamentals of computer architecture and how computers work, databases, SQL and accessing databases from R; In the face-to-face and onlnes classes we will do some hands-on data manipulation exercises. Extension content covering Python is also provided for students who wish to broaden their familiarity with current data science tools.

Extension content covering Python is also provided for students who wish to broaden their familiarity with current data science tools. in Visualisation and Communication of Health Data.

topics.name: Week 4 core material covers collaboration using git and GitHub, including collaborative report writing, as well as looking at creating effective tables for presenting results. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will look at visualising quantities and distributions, and practice that with some more hands-on ggplot2 (and optionally Python) coding exercises.
topics.description: Week 4 core material covers collaboration using git and GitHub, including collaborative report writing, as well as looking at creating effective tables for presenting results. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will look at visualising quantities and distributions, and practice that with some more hands-on ggplot2 (and optionally Python) coding exercises. in Visualisation and Communication of Health Data.

topics.name: Week 5 core material covers part 1 of visualising and mapping, how to display spatial and geographic data, including a review of the text "How to Lie with Maps" for negative examples of what not to do. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will examine incorporating time into charts -- that is, visualising trend data; as well as the uses and misuses of animation in data visualisation, with hands-on coding exercises to explore both.

topics.name: Week 7 core material looks at building interactive data-driven web applications (such as dashboards) using Shiny (part 1), using R and/or Python. topics.name: Week 8 core material covers part 2 of visualising and mapping. In the online and face-to-face tutorial sessions we will have another guest lecturer, Dr Mark Hanly, who will talk about communicating using story-telling, as well as through Markdown documents, web sites, pre-print papers and Shiny apps (and/or additional related topics). Hands-on exercises will involve construction of a brief story-telling (narrative) presentation or web page.

topics.name: Week 9 core material looks at building interactive data-driven web apps using Shiny (part 2). subtopics.description: Understanding how regular languages are closed under operations like union, concatenation, Kleene star, complement, and intersection.

subtopics.name: The Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
subtopics.description: Learning the formal statement of the pumping lemma and how it characterizes properties that all regular languages must satisfy.

subtopics.name: Proving Non-Regularity Using the Pumping Lemma
subtopics.description: Applying proof by contradiction and the pumping lemma to demonstrate that specific languages are not regular.

subtopics.name: Pushdown Automata and Formal Definition
subtopics.description: Understanding the structure, operation, and capabilities of PDAs including their formal definition, transitions, and stack manipulation.

subtopics.name: Context-Free Grammars and Normal Forms

subtopics.name: Ambiguity and Language Properties
subtopics.description: Identifying and resolving ambiguity in grammars, proving whether languages are context-free, and understanding limitations of CFLs in the Chomsky hierarchy.

subtopics.name: Turing Machine Fundamentals and Church-Turing Thesis
subtopics.description: Understanding the formal definition of Turing machines, their components, and the Church-Turing thesis as a foundational claim about effective computability.

subtopics.name: Decidability, Recognizability, and the Halting Problem
subtopics.description: Distinguishing between decidable and recognizable languages, understanding why the halting problem is undecidable, and implications for computational limits.

subtopics.name: Computational Universality and Reducibility
subtopics.description: Analyzing how universal Turing machines simulate other machines and using reduction techniques to prove undecidability of new problems.

subtopics.name: P and NP Complexity Classes
subtopics.description: Understanding the definitions, relationships, and characteristics of polynomial-time decidable (P) and polynomial-time verifiable (NP) problem classes.

subtopics.name: NP-Completeness and Reduction Techniques
subtopics.description: Exploring the concept of NP-complete problems, polynomial-time reductions, and how to prove NP-completeness using known complete problems.

subtopics.name: The Cook-Levin Theorem and Hardness
subtopics.description: Understanding the Cook-Levin theorem establishing SAT as NP-complete, and the broader implications for NP-hardness and computational hardness.

subtopics.name: Model Checking Fundamentals
subtopics.description: Core concepts and algorithms for automated verification of finite-state systems against formal specifications.

subtopics.name: Temporal Logic and Properties
subtopics.description: Specification of system behavior over time using temporal logics like LTL and CTL, including safety and liveness properties.

subtopics.name: Assertions and Invariants
subtopics.description: Methods for specifying and verifying properties that must hold at specific program points or throughout execution.

subtopics.name: Program Correctness and Verification
subtopics.description: Techniques and methodologies for proving that programs satisfy their specifications through formal methods.

subtopics.name: Type Systems and Static Analysis
subtopics.description: Formal approaches to detecting errors and guaranteeing program properties before execution through type checking and abstract analysis.

subtopics.name: Theorem Proving and Formal Semantics
subtopics.description: Using mathematical logic and formal semantics frameworks to mechanically verify complex system properties and program behaviors.

subtopics.name: Security Fundamentals and Socio-Technical Systems
subtopics.description: Core security concepts and the interaction between technical systems, people, and organizational processes in creating comprehensive security.

subtopics.name: Human Factors and Behavioral Economics in Security
subtopics.description: How cognitive biases, decision-making patterns, and economic incentives influence human security behavior and vulnerability to threats.

subtopics.name: Security Culture and Risk Perception
subtopics.description: The role of organizational culture, individual risk perception, and awareness in shaping security practices and compliance behaviors.

subtopics.name: Cognitive Biases in Security Decision-Making
subtopics.description: How systematic errors in thinking, such as confirmation bias and availability bias, affect security-related choices and judgments.

subtopics.name: Heuristics and Mental Shortcuts
subtopics.description: The role of mental shortcuts and rules of thumb in simplifying decision-making, including anchoring effects and their security implications.

subtopics.name: Password Behavior and User Authentication
subtopics.description: How cognitive biases influence password creation, reuse, and management practices, affecting overall security posture.

subtopics.name: Social Engineering Techniques and Attack Vectors
subtopics.description: Core methods used to manipulate people into divulging confidential information or performing security-compromising actions, including phishing, pretexting, and baiting.

subtopics.name: Psychological Principles and Manipulation Tactics
subtopics.description: Exploitation of cognitive biases and human psychology such as authority, urgency, scarcity, reciprocity, and trust to overcome rational decision-making.

subtopics.name: Authority Exploitation and Trust Manipulation
subtopics.description: Techniques that leverage perceived or impersonated authority figures and the manipulation of established trust relationships to gain unauthorized access or information.

subtopics.name: Password Creation and User Behavior
subtopics.description: Examination of how users create and manage passwords, including cognitive biases, memorability constraints, and common security pitfalls that lead to weak authentication.

subtopics.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Adoption and Usability
subtopics.description: Analysis of factors influencing user acceptance of MFA systems, the trade-offs between security strength and ease of use, and barriers to widespread adoption.

subtopics.name: Authentication Fatigue and Usability-Security Trade-offs
subtopics.description: Study of how repeated authentication demands affect user behavior, the cumulative burden of security measures, and design strategies to balance security requirements with user acceptance.

subtopics.name: Security Awareness Programs
subtopics.description: Design, implementation, and evaluation of training initiatives that educate employees about security risks, policies, and best practices.

subtopics.name: Behavioral Change and Compliance Motivation
subtopics.description: Psychological and organizational mechanisms that drive employees to adopt secure behaviors and maintain compliance with security policies.

subtopics.name: Insider Threats and Security Culture
subtopics.description: Understanding how organizational culture, employee engagement, and security practices influence the likelihood and impact of insider threats.

subtopics.name: Security Interface Design and Mental Models
subtopics.description: Principles of designing security interfaces that align with user mental models and cognitive processes to improve usability without compromising protection.

subtopics.name: Security Warnings and Notification Fatigue
subtopics.description: The psychology of security warnings, how users respond to alerts, and the challenge of maintaining effectiveness while avoiding habituation and warning fatigue.

subtopics.name: Accessible Security and Inclusive Design
subtopics.description: Designing security mechanisms that are usable by people with diverse abilities, including those with visual, auditory, motor, or cognitive disabilities.

subtopics.name: Privacy Paradox and Disclosure Behavior
subtopics.description: The disconnect between users' stated privacy concerns and their actual data disclosure practices, and the psychological factors that influence when people willingly share personal information.

subtopics.name: Trust Mechanisms and System Design
subtopics.description: How trust is established in digital systems through design choices, transparency practices, and user control mechanisms, and the role of trust in determining user acceptance of privacy-invasive services.

subtopics.name: Consent, Control and Regulatory Psychology
subtopics.description: The effectiveness and limitations of consent mechanisms, the psychological impact of perceived control over data, and how regulatory frameworks influence user behavior and organizational compliance practices.

subtopics.name: Designing for Human Error
subtopics.description: Principles and strategies for creating systems that anticipate, accommodate, and gracefully handle human mistakes rather than punishing users.

subtopics.name: Fail-Safe Defaults and Security by Design
subtopics.description: Implementation approaches that embed security into system architecture from inception, ensuring secure states are the default outcome when failures occur.

subtopics.name: User Feedback and Socio-Technical Integration
subtopics.description: Mechanisms for providing meaningful security feedback to users and aligning technical controls with organizational and human behavioral requirements.

subtopics.name: Integration of Human-Centric Security Concepts
subtopics.description: Synthesizing behavioral psychology, organizational culture, technology design, and policy frameworks to create comprehensive security approaches.

subtopics.name: Emerging Threats and AI's Role in Security Behavior
subtopics.description: Examining how artificial intelligence impacts both attacker strategies and defender capabilities, alongside new human-centered security challenges in digital environments.

subtopics.name: Ethical Considerations and Research Frontiers
subtopics.description: Exploring the ethical implications of security interventions, privacy concerns, and the future research directions in human-centric security.

subtopics.name: Recursion Fundamentals

subtopics.name: Algorithm Analysis and Big-O Notation
subtopics.description: Analyzing algorithm efficiency using Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta notation to classify time and space complexity.

subtopics.description: Solving recurrence relations using substitution, recursion trees, and the Master Theorem to determine recursive algorithm complexity.

subtopics.name: Comparison-Based Sorting
subtopics.description: Sorting algorithms that rely on comparing elements to determine their relative order, including bubble sort, insertion sort, merge sort, and quicksort.

subtopics.name: Time and Space Complexity Analysis
subtopics.description: Evaluating the performance characteristics of sorting algorithms in terms of best, average, and worst-case time complexity and auxiliary space requirements.

subtopics.name: Algorithm Selection and Optimization
subtopics.description: Choosing appropriate sorting algorithms based on input characteristics and implementing practical optimizations like pivot selection and hybrid approaches.

subtopics.name: Abstract Data Types (ADTs)
subtopics.description: Formal specifications of data structures that define operations and their behavior without implementation details.

subtopics.name: Binary Search Tree Properties

subtopics.description: Implementation and analysis of insertion, deletion, and search operations in binary search trees and their time complexities.

subtopics.name: Binary Search Tree Operations

subtopics.name: Graph Representations
subtopics.description: Different methods to represent graphs including adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and edge lists.

subtopics.description: Basic graph traversal algorithms such as breadth-first search and depth-first search with their applications.

subtopics.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
subtopics.description: A graph traversal algorithm that explores all vertices at the current depth level before moving to vertices at the next depth level, using a queue-based approach.

subtopics.name: Graph Problem Applications
subtopics.description: Practical applications of graph traversal and algorithms to solve problems such as cycle detection, topological sorting, and shortest paths.

subtopics.name: Graph Representations
subtopics.description: Understanding adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists for representing graphs in memory.

subtopics.name: Graph Traversal Algorithms
subtopics.description: Implementing and analyzing depth-first search (DFS) and breadth-first search (BFS) for exploring graph structures.

subtopics.name: Shortest Path Algorithms
subtopics.description: Applying Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford algorithms to find optimal paths in weighted graphs.

subtopics.name: Directed and Weighted Graphs
subtopics.description: Representation and properties of directed graphs with edge weights, including adjacency matrices and adjacency lists.

subtopics.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
subtopics.description: Single-source shortest path algorithm that greedily selects minimum distance vertices to find optimal paths in weighted graphs.

subtopics.name: Minimum Spanning Trees
subtopics.description: Subsets of edges connecting all vertices with minimum total weight, computed using algorithms like Kruskal's and Prim's.

subtopics.name: Hash Functions and Collision Resolution
subtopics.description: Methods for designing hash functions and handling collisions through chaining, open addressing, and double hashing.

subtopics.name: Load Factor and Dynamic Resizing
subtopics.description: Analysis of hash table performance metrics and strategies for maintaining efficiency through table resizing.

subtopics.name: Hash Table Implementation and Trade-offs
subtopics.description: Practical considerations in implementing hash tables including space complexity, average vs worst-case performance, and application selection.

subtopics.name: Priority Queues and Heap Operations

subtopics.name: Binary Heaps and Heapify
subtopics.description: Complete binary trees satisfying the heap property where parents have higher (max-heap) or lower (min-heap) priority than children, maintained through heapify operations.

subtopics.name: Tries and String Processing
subtopics.description: Tree-based data structures for efficient string storage and retrieval with O(m) operations where m is string length, commonly used for autocomplete and prefix matching.

subtopics.name: Time and Space Complexity Analysis
subtopics.description: Understanding Big O notation, asymptotic analysis, and comparing algorithm efficiency across different data structures and algorithmic paradigms.

subtopics.name: Graph Algorithms and Tree Traversals
subtopics.description: Mastering depth-first search, breadth-first search, shortest path algorithms, and their applications in solving real-world problems.

subtopics.name: Advanced Data Structures and Optimization Techniques
subtopics.description: Exploring balanced trees, hash tables, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms to solve complex computational problems efficiently.

subtopics.name: Causes and Categories of Software Failures
subtopics.description: Understanding why software fails through analysis of defects, environmental factors, and human error in development and deployment.

subtopics.name: Verification vs. Validation Fundamentals
subtopics.description: Distinguishing between verification (building the product right) and validation (building the right product) as core quality assurance concepts.

subtopics.name: The V-Model and Its Application
subtopics.description: Exploring the V-model's structure as a testing and development framework that maps testing activities to corresponding development phases.

subtopics.name: Boundary Value Analysis
subtopics.description: A black-box testing technique that focuses on testing values at the edges of input domains, including minimum, maximum, and just beyond these boundaries.

subtopics.name: Equivalence Class Partitioning
subtopics.description: A method that divides input data into groups where all members are expected to behave identically, reducing test cases while maintaining comprehensive coverage.

subtopics.name: Decision Tables and Cause-Effect Graphing
subtopics.description: Systematic techniques for modeling complex business rules and their combinations to generate comprehensive test cases that exercise all logical branches and conditions.

subtopics.name: Pairwise and t-way Testing
subtopics.description: Combinatorial testing technique that ensures all pairs (or t-tuples) of parameter values are covered at least once to reduce test suite size while maintaining effectiveness.

subtopics.name: Statement and Branch Coverage
subtopics.description: Structural coverage criteria measuring the percentage of executable statements and decision branches executed during test execution.

subtopics.name: Modified Condition/Decision Coverage (MC/DC)
subtopics.description: A rigorous structural coverage criterion requiring that each condition independently affects the outcome of its decision while varying other conditions.

subtopics.name: Path Coverage and Basis Paths
subtopics.description: Techniques for identifying and testing independent execution paths through a program using control flow analysis.

subtopics.name: Data-Flow Testing
subtopics.description: Testing strategy that tracks variable definitions and uses throughout program execution to identify data-flow anomalies and coverage gaps.

subtopics.name: Software Complexity Metrics
subtopics.description: Quantitative measures such as cyclomatic complexity and coupling that assess code complexity and predict testability and maintainability.

subtopics.name: Unit Testing Fundamentals
subtopics.description: Core principles of unit testing including test isolation, assertion frameworks, and writing effective test cases for individual software components.

subtopics.name: Test Scaffolding and Mocking
subtopics.description: Techniques for isolating units under test using test doubles such as mocks, stubs, and fakes to control external dependencies and verify behavior.

subtopics.name: Integration Testing Strategies
subtopics.description: Approaches for testing interactions between multiple components including big-bang, incremental, and sandwich integration testing methods.

subtopics.name: System Testing and Integration
subtopics.description: Testing complete, integrated systems to verify end-to-end functionality and interaction between components.

subtopics.name: Model-Based Testing and Non-Functional Testing
subtopics.description: Using formal models to generate test cases and evaluating system properties like performance, security, and usability.

subtopics.name: The Test Oracle Problem
subtopics.description: The challenge of determining whether test outputs are correct when expected results are unknown or difficult to define.

subtopics.name: Mutation Testing Fundamentals
subtopics.description: Mutation testing involves introducing small deliberate changes (mutations) to source code to evaluate test suite effectiveness by measuring kill rates.

subtopics.name: Mutation Operators and Mutant Classification
subtopics.description: Mutation operators are transformations applied to code (arithmetic operator changes, boundary modifications, etc.) and mutants are classified as killed, survived, or equivalent.

subtopics.name: Property-Based Testing Principles
subtopics.description: Property-based testing generates multiple test cases from properties that should hold for all inputs, enabling discovery of edge cases and improving test coverage.

subtopics.name: Fuzz Testing Fundamentals and Principles
subtopics.description: Core concepts of fuzz testing including mutation-based and generation-based approaches for discovering software vulnerabilities.

subtopics.name: American Fuzzy Lop (AFL) Architecture and Operations
subtopics.description: AFL's design components including instrumentation, genetic algorithms, and feedback mechanisms for efficient bug discovery.

subtopics.name: AFL Implementation, Coverage-Guided Fuzzing, and Practical Applications
subtopics.description: Practical usage of AFL tools, coverage-guided strategies, and techniques for maximizing bug detection in real-world software.

subtopics.name: Adaptive Random Testing (ART)
subtopics.description: A testing technique that selects test cases non-uniformly to maximize failure detection by maintaining distance between test cases in the input domain.

subtopics.name: Genetic Algorithms in Software Testing
subtopics.description: Evolutionary algorithms that generate test cases by simulating natural selection, mutation, and crossover to optimize test suite effectiveness.

subtopics.name: Testing Under Budget Constraints
subtopics.description: Strategies for allocating limited testing resources to maximize defect detection while respecting time, cost, and personnel constraints.

subtopics.name: Design Goals and Quality Attributes
subtopics.description: Core objectives in software design including flexibility, reusability, maintainability, and extensibility.

subtopics.name: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
subtopics.description: A class should have only one reason to change, meaning it should have only one responsibility or concern.

subtopics.name: SOLID Principles Overview
subtopics.description: Five fundamental principles (Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion) that guide object-oriented design.

subtopics.name: OOP Principles and Encapsulation

subtopics.name: Classes, Interfaces, and Relationships

subtopics.name: UML Diagrams and Design Documentation

subtopics.name: Singleton Pattern

subtopics.name: Factory and Abstract Factory Patterns
subtopics.description: Define interfaces for creating objects without specifying their concrete classes, enabling flexible object creation and decoupling client code from implementation details.

subtopics.name: Builder Pattern and Object Creation Strategies
subtopics.description: Separates the construction of complex objects from their representation, allowing step-by-step creation and comparison of different instantiation approaches.

subtopics.name: Adapter and Bridge Patterns
subtopics.description: Techniques for connecting incompatible interfaces and separating abstraction from implementation to enable flexibility and independent evolution.

subtopics.name: Composite and Decorator Patterns
subtopics.description: Patterns for building hierarchical structures and adding responsibilities to objects dynamically while maintaining the same interface.

subtopics.name: Facade and Proxy Patterns
subtopics.description: Structural patterns that provide simplified interfaces to complex subsystems and control access to objects respectively.

subtopics.name: Observer Pattern
subtopics.description: Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects where changes to a subject automatically notify all registered observers.

subtopics.name: Strategy and Command Patterns

subtopics.name: State and Template Method Patterns
subtopics.description: State allows objects to alter behavior when internal state changes, while Template Method defines algorithm structure in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps.

subtopics.name: Design Pattern Selection and Trade-offs
subtopics.description: Evaluating when to apply specific design patterns and understanding their advantages and disadvantages in different contexts.

subtopics.name: Object-Oriented Principles Review
subtopics.description: Reinforcing SOLID principles, inheritance, polymorphism, and composition to support good software design decisions.

subtopics.name: Architectural Patterns and System Design

subtopics.name: Iterator and Visitor Patterns
subtopics.description: Structural approaches to traversing and operating on collections without exposing their internal structure or tight coupling to algorithms.

subtopics.name: Chain of Responsibility and Mediator
subtopics.description: Patterns for managing communication flow and request handling through chains of handlers or centralized coordinators.

subtopics.name: Pattern Selection and Trade-offs
subtopics.description: Analyzing when to apply each behavioral pattern and understanding their architectural implications and performance considerations.

subtopics.name: Model-View-Controller (MVC) Pattern
subtopics.description: An architectural pattern that separates an application into three interconnected components to organize code and improve maintainability.

subtopics.name: Layered Architecture
subtopics.description: An architectural approach that organizes the system into horizontal layers where each layer provides services to the layer above it.

subtopics.name: Separation of Concerns
subtopics.description: A design principle that divides a system into distinct sections, each addressing a specific concern or responsibility.

subtopics.name: Code Smells & Detection
subtopics.description: Identifying patterns in code that indicate deeper design problems such as duplicate code, long methods, and inappropriate intimacy between classes.

subtopics.name: Refactoring Techniques & Patterns
subtopics.description: Applying systematic transformations like Extract Method, Move Class, and Simplify Conditional to improve code structure without changing behavior.

subtopics.name: Testing Strategies & Technical Debt Management
subtopics.description: Using unit tests and regression testing to safely refactor code while identifying and prioritizing technical debt reduction.

subtopics.name: Design Pattern Combinations
subtopics.description: Understanding how multiple design patterns work together to solve complex architectural problems.

subtopics.name: Real-World Architecture Decisions
subtopics.description: Evaluating trade-offs and constraints when selecting architectural patterns for production systems.

subtopics.name: Course Synthesis and Integration
subtopics.description: Applying accumulated knowledge of OOP, design principles, and patterns to comprehensive system design scenarios.

subtopics.description: Understanding the layered architecture of database management systems including storage, query processing, and transaction management components.

subtopics.name: Data Models and the Relational Model

subtopics.name: Database Concepts and Advantages

subtopics.name: Relational Model Fundamentals

subtopics.name: Keys and Integrity Constraints

subtopics.description: Selecting appropriate index types and structures to optimize query performance based on cost models and cardinality estimation.

subtopics.name: Query Optimization Techniques
subtopics.description: Applying heuristic and cost-based optimization methods to transform logical query plans into efficient physical execution plans.

subtopics.name: Relational Algebra and Query Optimization
subtopics.description: Understanding query execution plans, optimization techniques, and how to evaluate relational algebra expressions for efficiency.

subtopics.name: Transaction Management and ACID Properties
subtopics.description: Concepts of atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, concurrency control, and recovery mechanisms in database systems.

subtopics.name: Indexing Strategies and Physical Database Design
subtopics.description: Selection and implementation of appropriate index types, trade-offs between query performance and storage overhead, and schema design considerations.

subtopics.name: ACID Properties and Transaction Semantics
subtopics.description: Fundamental guarantees that transactions must satisfy to maintain database consistency and reliability.

subtopics.name: Locking Protocols and Concurrency Control

subtopics.name: Document Databases and Data Models

subtopics.name: Virtual Memory and Page Replacement

subtopics.name: Instruction Set Architecture and Processor Design

questions.question: Which of the following registers is used to store the return address when a function is called using the `jal` instruction?
choices: $ra
$sp
questions.explanation: $ra (return address register) is specifically designated to hold the address of the instruction following a `jal` call, allowing the function to return to the caller.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the $zero register in MIPS?
choices: To store temporary calculation results
To always contain the value 0 and cannot be written to
To hold function arguments passed from the caller
To store saved values that must be preserved across function calls
questions.explanation: $zero is hardwired to always read as 0; any write to it is ignored. This makes it useful for operations like clearing a register or implementing logical operations.

questions.question: How many temporary registers ($t0-$t9) are available in the standard MIPS register file?
questions.explanation: The temporary registers range from $t0 to $t9 inclusive, providing exactly 10 temporary registers for use in calculations without preservation requirements.

questions.question: A function receives three integer arguments. Which registers would these arguments be passed in according to the standard MIPS calling convention?
questions.explanation: In MIPS calling conventions, the first four function arguments are passed in registers $a0, $a1, $a2, and $a3; the first three arguments therefore use $a0, $a1, and $a2.

questions.question:
Consider this code fragment:
```
addi $t0, $zero, 5
addi $t1, $zero, 3
add $s0, $t0, $t1
```
What value does $s0 contain after execution?
questions.explanation: $t0 is loaded with 5, $t1 with 3, and then $s0 is assigned the sum of $t0 and $t1, resulting in 8.

questions.question: A function must preserve the value in $s3 across a function call. Which of the following best describes why $s3 is used instead of a temporary register?
choices: $s registers are faster than $t registers
$s registers must be saved and restored by the called function, ensuring the caller's value is preserved
$s3 is never used by other functions
Temporary registers cannot hold values larger than 16 bits
questions.explanation: The MIPS calling convention specifies that $s0-$s7 are 'saved' registers; the called function is responsible for saving and restoring them, allowing the caller to rely on their preservation.

questions.question:
A programmer writes the following code intending to set $t0 to 0:
```
addi $t0, $zero, 0
```
Which registers are read from in this instruction?
choices: Only $t0
Only $zero
$zero and $t0
Neither register is read
questions.explanation: The `addi` instruction reads only the first source register ($zero in this case); $t0 is the destination and is written to, not read from.

questions.question: A function receives 6 integer arguments according to MIPS conventions. Where is the 5th argument located?
choices: $sp+16 (on the stack)
questions.explanation: Only the first 4 arguments use $a0-$a3; the 5th and subsequent arguments are passed on the stack, typically at offsets from $sp.

questions.question: Consider a scenario where $v0 contains a return value from a function, and immediately afterward the calling code executes `addi $v0, $v0, 1`. What subtle issue might arise if the called function was supposed to return a 32-bit result?
choices: $v0 cannot hold 32-bit values
If the result overflows 32 bits after the increment, the overflow is silently ignored in standard MIPS without an exception
$v1 must be used alongside $v0 to hold 64-bit values, but the code only uses $v0
The `addi` instruction cannot operate on return values
questions.explanation: In MIPS, a 64-bit return value uses both $v0 and $v1 together; incrementing only $v0 ignores $v1 and will produce an incorrect result for large values, requiring both registers to be updated together.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction loads the immediate value 100 into register $t0?
choices: load $t0, 100
addi $t0, $zero, 100
questions.explanation: The 'li' (load immediate) pseudo-instruction is the standard way to load a constant value directly into a register. While addi can achieve the same effect, li is the idiomatic choice.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for moving the value in $s0 to $s1?
choices: move $s1, $s0
mov $s0, $s1
li $s1, $s0
add $s0, $s1, $zero
questions.explanation: The 'move' pseudo-instruction copies the value from the source register ($s0) to the destination register ($s1). MIPS uses 'move' not 'mov', and the destination comes first.

questions.question: Which instruction correctly adds the contents of $t1 and $t2, storing the result in $t0?
choices: add $t0, $t1, $t2
add $t1, $t2, $t0
addi $t0, $t1, $t2
questions.explanation: The 'add' instruction takes the destination register first, followed by two source registers in order. The syntax is 'add dest, src1, src2'.

questions.question:
What will be the value in $t0 after these instructions execute?
li $t0, 50
addi $t0, $t0, 25
questions.explanation: The 'li' loads 50 into $t0. The 'addi' (add immediate) then adds 25 to the current value of $t0, resulting in 75.

questions.question:
Trace the following code:
li $s0, 10
li $s1, 3
sub $s2, $s0, $s1
mul $t0, $s2, 2
What is the final value in $t0?
questions.explanation: First, $s0=10 and $s1=3. Then $s2 = 10-3 = 7. Finally, $t0 = 7*2 = 14.

questions.question:
Consider this sequence:
li $t1, -5
addi $t1, $t1, 10
sub $t2, $t1, 3
What is the value in $t2?
questions.explanation: $t1 starts at -5, then -5+10=5. Then $t2=5-3=2. The instruction correctly handles negative immediates and performs subtraction left-to-right.

questions.question:
What is the result of executing this code if $a0 initially contains 0x80000000 (the most negative 32-bit signed integer)?
add $a1, $a0, $a0
choices: Overflow occurs; result is unpredictable
$a1 contains 0x00000000
questions.explanation: Adding 0x80000000 to itself causes a signed integer overflow in 32-bit MIPS arithmetic. The result wraps around and the overflow flag is set, making the exact result dependent on how the processor handles the exception.

questions.question: Which of these sequences correctly computes $t0 = ($s0 × 4) + 12?
choices:
mul $t0, $s0, 4
addi $t0, $t0, 12

addi $t0, $s0, 12
mul $t0, $t0, 4

li $t0, 12
mul $t0, $s0, 4
add $t0, $t0, $t0

mul $t0, $s0, 4
add $t0, $s0, 12
questions.explanation: First multiply $s0 by 4 and store in $t0, then add 12 to $t0. The other options either apply operations in the wrong order or compute incorrect intermediate values.

questions.question:
After executing these instructions, what is in $t3?
li $t0, 100
li $t1, 50
sub $t2, $t0, $t1
mul $t3, $t2, $t2
addi $t3, $t3, -2500
questions.explanation: $t2 = 100-50 = 50. Then $t3 = 50*50 = 2500. Finally, $t3 = 2500 + (-2500) = 0. The sequence carefully sets up a computation that results in zero after the final adjustment.

questions.question: Which syscall number is used to print an integer in MIPS?
questions.explanation: Syscall 1 is the print_int syscall. The integer to be printed must be in $a0 before the syscall is invoked.

questions.question: What must be placed in the $a0 register before calling the print_string syscall?
choices: The memory address of the string to print
The length of the string
The ASCII value of the first character
The string itself (copied into the register)
questions.explanation: The print_string syscall ($v0 = 4) requires the memory address (pointer) of the string in $a0, not the string data itself.

questions.question: Which syscall is used to read an integer from user input?
questions.explanation: Syscall 5 is read_int, which reads an integer from standard input and returns it in $v0.

questions.question:
Consider the following MIPS code:

li $v0, 1
li $a0, 42
syscall

What will be printed to the console?
choices: Nothing (syscall fails)
questions.explanation: This code sets $v0 to 1 (print_int) and $a0 to 42, then calls syscall. The output will be 42.

questions.question: Which register receives the value returned by a read_int syscall?
choices: $ra
questions.explanation: The read_int syscall ($v0 = 5) returns the input integer in $v0, from which it must be copied to another register if needed.

questions.question:
Consider this code segment:

li $v0, 4
la $a0, msg
syscall
li $v0, 1
li $a0, 100
syscall

Assuming 'msg' is the label for the string "Number: ", what is the output?
choices: Number: 100
Number:
questions.explanation: The first syscall prints the string at address msg ("Number: "), and the second syscall prints the integer 100. The output is the string followed by the number.

questions.question: What is the syscall number for the exit syscall?
questions.explanation: Syscall 10 is the exit syscall, which terminates the program. Optionally, $a0 can contain an exit code.

questions.question:
A programmer writes the following code to print an integer and then exit:

li $v0, 1
li $a0, 7
syscall
li $v0, 10
syscall

What is the potential issue with this code?
choices: The exit syscall should come before print_int
The $a0 register is not preserved between syscalls, so exit will not work correctly
There is no issue; this code is correct
The print_int syscall modifies $v0, so it cannot be reset to 10
questions.explanation: This code is correct. The print_int syscall prints 7, and then the exit syscall terminates the program. Each syscall sets $v0 independently.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code:

li $v0, 5
syscall
move $a0, $v0
li $v0, 1
syscall

Assuming the user inputs 25, what will be displayed?
choices: The program will crash
Nothing will be displayed
questions.explanation: The first syscall reads an integer (25) into $v0. The move instruction copies this value to $a0. The second syscall prints the value in $a0, which is 25.

questions.question: In a MIPS program, which section contains variable declarations and data initialization?
choices: .text
.data
.code
.stack
questions.explanation: The .data section is used for declaring and initializing variables and global data. The .text section contains executable instructions.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to declare a 32-bit word in the .data section of a MIPS program?
choices: var: .int 5
var: .word 5
var: .long 5
var: w 5
questions.explanation: In MIPS assembly, .word is the directive for declaring 32-bit integers. .int is not standard MIPS syntax; .long and 'w' are incorrect.

questions.question: Which register is typically used as the entry point for a sequential MIPS program execution?
choices: $zero
$ra
$pc
main
questions.explanation: The program begins execution at the label 'main' in the .text section. While $pc (program counter) tracks execution, 'main' is the named entry point where sequential execution starts.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code segment:
.data
x: .word 10
y: .word 20
.text
main:
  lw $t0, x
  lw $t1, y
  add $t2, $t0, $t1

After execution, what value is in $t2?
choices: Undefined (x and y are not initialized)
questions.explanation: The lw instructions load x (10) into $t0 and y (20) into $t1. The add instruction computes $t0 + $t1 = 10 + 20 = 30, storing the result in $t2.

questions.question: A MIPS sequential program loads a value from memory using 'lw $t0, 0($sp)'. Which of the following best describes what this instruction does?
choices: Loads a word from the address stored in $t0 into memory
Loads a word from the address pointed to by $sp into $t0
Loads a word from $sp offset by 0 bytes into $t0
Stores the word in $t0 to the address in $sp
questions.explanation: The lw instruction loads a word from memory. The operand 0($sp) means the memory address is $sp + 0, and the loaded value goes into $t0. This is correct register-indirect addressing with offset.

questions.question:
In a sequential MIPS program, you declare an array in .data as:
arr: .word 5, 10, 15, 20

What is the memory offset to access the third element (value 15) from the label 'arr'?
choices: 4 bytes
6 bytes
8 bytes
12 bytes
questions.explanation: Each .word is 4 bytes. The third element is at index 2 (0-indexed), so offset = 2 × 4 = 8 bytes from the label 'arr'.

questions.question:
A MIPS sequential program contains:
.data
x: .word -5
.text
main:
  lw $t0, x
  add $t1, $t0, $t0
  add $t2, $t1, $t0

What is the final value in $t2, considering two's complement representation?
questions.explanation: x = -5 is loaded into $t0. Then $t1 = $t0 + $t0 = -5 + (-5) = -10. Finally, $t2 = $t1 + $t0 = -10 + (-5) = -15 in two's complement arithmetic.

questions.question: A MIPS program declares multiple variables but a sequential program segment only loads and uses one. After execution, what is guaranteed about the unused variables in memory?
choices: They are automatically freed and their memory is reclaimed
They retain their initialized values exactly as declared in .data
They are overwritten by the program's stack
Their values depend on previous program runs
questions.explanation: In MIPS, variables declared in .data are stored in the static data segment and retain their initialized values throughout program execution unless explicitly modified by load/store instructions. Unused variables are not freed or modified automatically.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS sequential program:
.data
result: .word 0
.text
main:
  li $t0, 7
  li $t1, 3
  sub $t2, $t0, $t1
  sw $t2, result

Assuming 'result' is at memory address 0x10000000, what does the sw instruction do?
choices: Stores the word in result register to address in $t2
Stores the word in $t2 (value 4) to memory address 0x10000000
Stores the word from memory at 0x10000000 to $t2
Stores the word in $t0 minus $t1 to register result
questions.explanation: The sw instruction stores the word in $t2 (which contains 7 - 3 = 4) to the memory address labeled 'result' (0x10000000). The instruction does not use $t2 as an address; it uses $t2 as the source value.

questions.question: What does the MIPS instruction `beq $t0, $t1, label` do?
choices: Branches to label if $t0 equals $t1
Branches to label if $t0 is not equal to $t1
Branches to label if $t0 is less than $t1
Branches to label if $t0 is greater than $t1
questions.explanation: beq stands for 'branch if equal'. It compares two registers and branches only when they contain the same value.

questions.question: Which MIPS instruction branches when two registers are NOT equal?
choices: beq
bne
blt
bge
questions.explanation: bne stands for 'branch if not equal' and is used to branch when the condition $rs ≠ $rt is true.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax for a MIPS branch instruction that branches if $s0 < $s1?
choices: blt $s0, $s1, target
blt $s0 $s1 target
blt target, $s0, $s1
b< $s0, $s1, target
questions.explanation: The correct MIPS syntax for blt (branch if less than) is: blt $rs, $rt, label, where registers are separated by commas and the label comes last.

questions.question:
Trace the following code. If $t0 = 5 and $t1 = 5, which instruction executes immediately after `beq $t0, $t1, skip`?

beq $t0, $t1, skip
addi $t2, $t2, 1
skip: addi $t3, $t3, 2
choices: addi $t2, $t2, 1
addi $t3, $t3, 2
beq $t0, $t1, skip (executes again)
The program terminates
questions.explanation: Since $t0 equals $t1, the beq condition is true, so the branch is taken to the skip label, executing `addi $t3, $t3, 2` next, skipping the `addi $t2, $t2, 1` instruction.

questions.question:
Trace the following code. If $a0 = 10 and $a1 = 7, what is the final value of $v0?

bgt $a0, $a1, greater
addi $v0, $zero, 0
j end
greater: addi $v0, $zero, 1
end:
questions.explanation: Since $a0 (10) is greater than $a1 (7), the bgt condition is true, so execution branches to 'greater' and $v0 is set to 1.

questions.question:
What will be the result after executing this code if $t0 = 3 and $t1 = 8?

bne $t0, $t1, notequal
addi $t2, $zero, 5
j done
notequal: addi $t2, $zero, 10
done:
questions.explanation: Since $t0 (3) is not equal to $t1 (8), bne branches to 'notequal', setting $t2 to 10 and skipping the instruction that would set it to 5.

questions.question: Consider this code segment with $t0 = -5 (in two's complement). What happens at `blt $t0, $zero, negative`?
choices: The branch is not taken because -5 is represented as a large unsigned number
The branch is taken because -5 is less than 0
The branch is taken because $zero is always larger than any register
The instruction causes an undefined behavior in MIPS
questions.explanation: blt performs a signed comparison. Since -5 (in two's complement) is indeed less than 0, the branch is taken. MIPS correctly interprets negative numbers in signed comparisons.

questions.question: What is the critical difference in behavior between `ble $s0, $s1, label` and `ble $s1, $s0, label`?
choices: They behave identically; the order of operands does not matter
The first branches if $s0 ≤ $s1; the second branches if $s1 ≤ $s0
The first branches if $s0 ≤ $s1; the second branches if $s0 ≥ $s1
MIPS does not support ble with reversed operands
questions.explanation: The ble instruction compares $rs ≤ $rt. In `ble $s0, $s1, label`, it checks $s0 ≤ $s1, but in `ble $s1, $s0, label`, it checks $s1 ≤ $s0, which is equivalent to $s0 ≥ $s1.

questions.question: A programmer writes: `bge $t0, $t1, skip` where $t0 = 0x80000000 (as a 32-bit signed integer, this is -2147483648). If $t1 = 1, will the branch be taken?
choices: Yes, because 0x80000000 is larger when interpreted as unsigned
No, because -2147483648 is less than 1 in signed arithmetic
Yes, because the comparison uses unsigned arithmetic by default
No, because $t1 must be initialized before comparison
questions.explanation: bge performs signed comparison. In signed two's complement arithmetic, 0x80000000 represents -2147483648, which is less than 1, so the branch is NOT taken.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the primary difference between the `j` instruction and the `jal` instruction?
choices: `jal` saves the return address in $ra before jumping, while `j` does not
`j` saves the return address in $ra before jumping, while `jal` does not
`jal` can only jump to labels, while `j` can jump to any address
Both instructions are identical; `jal` is just an alternative mnemonic for `j`
questions.explanation: `jal` (jump and link) is designed for function calls and automatically stores the return address (next instruction's address) in $ra, enabling the function to return. `j` performs an unconditional jump without saving any return address.

questions.question: Which instruction is used to return from a function that was called using `jal`?
choices: `j $ra`
`jr $ra`
`jal $ra`
`return $ra`
questions.explanation: `jr` (jump register) jumps to the address stored in a register. Since `jal` saves the return address in $ra, `jr $ra` is the standard way to return from a function.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the correct syntax for defining a label?
choices: `label: instruction`
`@label instruction`
`#label instruction`
`[label] instruction`
questions.explanation: MIPS labels are defined by placing an identifier followed by a colon (`:`) at the beginning of a line. This label can then be used as the target of jump instructions.

questions.question:
Consider the following MIPS code segment. What value will be in $v0 after execution?
```
jal func
addi $v0, $zero, 5
j end
func: addi $v0, $zero, 10
jr $ra
end: addi $v0, $v0, 3
```
questions.explanation: `jal func` calls the function, setting $v0 to 10 and saving the return address. `jr $ra` returns to the instruction after `jal`, which is `addi $v0, $v0, 3`. This adds 3 to 10, resulting in 13.

questions.question:
Trace through this MIPS code. How many times will the instruction at `loop:` be executed before the program reaches `done:`?
```
addi $t0, $zero, 3
loop: addi $t0, $t0, -1
bne $t0, $zero, loop
done: addi $v0, $zero, 0
```
choices: 2 times
3 times
4 times
1 time
questions.explanation: $t0 starts at 3. The loop decrements $t0 by 1 each iteration (3→2→1→0). The `bne` branches back while $t0 is not zero, so the loop executes 3 times total before $t0 becomes 0 and the branch fails.

questions.question: What will happen if you execute `jr $zero` in a MIPS program?
choices: The program will jump to address 0, likely causing a crash or undefined behavior
The program will halt gracefully
The instruction will be skipped
A compile error will be generated
questions.explanation: `jr` jumps to the address stored in the register. Since $zero always contains 0, `jr $zero` attempts to jump to address 0, which is not a valid program address and will cause a runtime error or crash.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code with nested function calls. After `jal func2` completes and control returns to `main`, what is in $ra?
```
main: jal func1
j end
func1: jal func2
jr $ra
func2: addi $v0, $zero, 5
jr $ra
end:
```
choices: The address of the `j end` instruction
The address of the `jal func2` instruction
The address of the `jr $ra` instruction in func1
Undefined; $ra is not modified by nested calls
questions.explanation: When `jal func1` executes, $ra is set to the address of `j end`. When `func1` calls `jal func2`, $ra is overwritten with the return address within func1. After func2 returns, func1 uses `jr $ra` to return to the saved address (`j end`), but $ra now contains func1's return address.

questions.question:
What is the critical issue with this code, and why might it fail?
```
loop: addi $t0, $t0, 1
addi $t1, $t1, 1
j loop
```
choices: The code is syntactically correct but creates an infinite loop with no exit condition
The `j` instruction syntax is incorrect; it should be `j $t0`
Labels cannot be used with `j`; use `jr` instead
The registers $t0 and $t1 are not initialized, causing undefined behavior
questions.explanation: While syntactically valid, this code unconditionally jumps back to `loop` with no branch condition or break mechanism, creating an infinite loop from which the program cannot escape.

questions.question: In a MIPS implementation, when `jal` executes, the return address saved in $ra is the address of which instruction?
choices: The `jal` instruction itself
The instruction immediately following the `jal` instruction
The label that `jal` is jumping to
The instruction at the end of the called function
questions.explanation: `jal` saves the Program Counter of the next instruction (PC + 4 in a 4-byte instruction architecture) so that when the called function executes `jr $ra`, control returns to the instruction after the `jal` call, not to the `jal` instruction itself.

questions.question: In MIPS, which branch instruction should be used to jump to a label if two registers are NOT equal?
choices: bne $s0, $s1, label
beq $s0, $s1, label
bne $s0, $s1, $s2
jne $s0, $s1, label
questions.explanation: bne (branch not equal) jumps to the label if the two register values are different. beq branches on equality, and jne is not a valid MIPS instruction.

questions.question: What is the correct structure for translating an if-else statement into MIPS?
choices: Use beq/bne to jump to else label if condition is false, execute if block, then jump over else block to end label
Use beq/bne to jump to if label if condition is true, skip to else, then jump to end
Use only jumps without any labels
Use beq to jump to else only if the condition is true
questions.explanation: The standard pattern branches to the else label when the condition is false, executes the if-block, then jumps to the end to skip the else block. This avoids executing both blocks.

questions.question: In MIPS, what does the label syntax represent in a conditional branch?
choices: A memory address in the code where execution should jump to
A variable that stores a branch condition
A register that holds the branch destination
A comment explaining the branch purpose
questions.explanation: Labels in MIPS represent symbolic names for memory addresses in the code. When a branch instruction is executed, it jumps to the instruction at the labeled address.

questions.question: Consider the C code: if (a > b) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; }. In MIPS, if a and b are in $s0 and $s1 respectively, which instruction should come first after loading the values?
choices: slt $t0, $s1, $s0  (to check if b < a)
slt $t0, $s0, $s1  (to check if a < b)
beq $s0, $s1, else_label
addi $s0, $s0, 1
questions.explanation: To check if a > b, we use slt $t0, $s1, $s0 which sets $t0=1 if $s1 < $s0 (i.e., b < a, which means a > b). This sets up the condition for the subsequent branch.

questions.question:
Trace the following MIPS code. Assume $s0 = 5 and $s1 = 3. What is the value of $s2 after execution?
  slt $t0, $s1, $s0
  beq $t0, $zero, else_label
  addi $s2, $zero, 10
  j end_label
else_label:
  addi $s2, $zero, 20
end_label:
questions.explanation: slt sets $t0=1 because 3 < 5. beq does not branch since $t0 ≠ $zero. So the if-block executes, setting $s2=10. The else block is skipped.

questions.question: In translating if (x != 0) in MIPS, which approach correctly checks the condition? Assume x is in $s0.
choices: Use bne $s0, $zero, if_label to jump into the if-block when x is non-zero
Use beq $s0, $zero, if_label to jump into the if-block when x is non-zero
Use slt $t0, $s0, $zero and then beq to check the condition
Use addi to add 1 to $s0 and then jump
questions.explanation: bne (branch not equal) jumps to if_label when $s0 ≠ $zero, which is exactly when x != 0 is true. This directly implements the condition without extra setup.

questions.question:
What is the critical error in the following MIPS if-else translation?
  beq $s0, $s1, else_label
  addi $s2, $zero, 1
else_label:
  addi $s2, $zero, 2
choices: Missing a jump statement to skip the else block after the if block executes
The beq instruction is backwards and should be bne
The labels are not defined properly in memory
The else_label comes after the else block instead of before it
questions.explanation: After executing the if-block (addi $s2, $zero, 1), control falls through to else_label and executes the else block, overwriting $s2. A j end_label is needed after the if-block to skip the else.

questions.question: Consider nested if-else: if (a > 0) { if (b < 10) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; } } else { x = 3; }. How many labels are minimally required for correct MIPS translation?
choices: 4 (labels for: outer else, inner if, inner else, end)
3 (labels for: else, inner else, end)
2 (labels for: else, end)
5 (labels for: outer if, outer else, inner if, inner else, end)
questions.explanation: We need: outer_else (jump if a ≤ 0), inner_else (jump if b ≥ 10 inside outer if), end_label (skip remaining code after any branch). The fourth label accounts for the structure of nested conditions.

questions.question: Assume a MIPS if-else translates to: beq $s0, $zero, else_L; addi $s1, $s1, 5; j end_L; else_L: addi $s1, $s1, 10; end_L:. If this runs twice in a loop with $s0 = 5 initially, what is $s1 after two iterations starting from $s1 = 0?
questions.explanation: Each iteration: $s0 = 5 (not zero), so beq doesn't jump. The if-block executes: $s1 += 5. After two iterations: 0 + 5 + 5 = 10. The else block is never executed because $s0 remains 5.

questions.question: In MIPS assembly, which instruction is most commonly used to implement the condition check in a while loop?
choices: beq (branch if equal)
add (add)
sw (store word)
lw (load word)
questions.explanation: Branch instructions like beq are used to evaluate loop conditions and control whether the loop body executes or the loop exits. Load and store are for memory operations, and add is for arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the label at the beginning of a while loop in MIPS?
choices: To mark where the loop condition is checked so it can be jumped back to
To declare a variable in the loop
To allocate memory for the loop
To increment the loop counter automatically
questions.explanation: Labels mark positions in code that branch instructions can jump to. In loops, the label at the start allows the code to jump back and re-evaluate the condition.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly translates a for loop increment `i++` in MIPS?
choices: addi $t0, $t0, 1
subi $t0, $t0, 1
beq $t0, $t1, loop_end
j $t0
questions.explanation: addi (add immediate) with 1 increments a register by 1. subi decrements, beq is a branch, and j jumps unconditionally—none increment properly.

questions.question: Consider this while loop: `while (x < 10) { x++; }` where x is in $t0. After the condition `slt $t1, $t0, 10` is executed, what does $t1 contain if x = 7?
choices: 1 (true)
0 (false)
questions.explanation: slt (set less than) sets the destination register to 1 if the first operand is less than the second, and 0 otherwise. Since 7 < 10, $t1 is set to 1.

questions.question:
What is the output of this MIPS loop snippet if $t0 starts at 5?

loop: addi $t0, $t0, -1
bne $t0, $zero, loop
addi $t1, $t1, 1

How many times does the addi $t1, $t1, 1 execute?
choices: 5 times
4 times
6 times
1 time
questions.explanation: The loop decrements $t0 from 5 to 4, 3, 2, 1, then 0, exiting when $t0 equals zero. This happens 5 times, so addi $t1 executes 5 times.

questions.question: Consider translating `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)` into MIPS. Which statement about the loop structure is correct?
choices: The initialization happens before the loop, the condition is checked at the start of each iteration, and the increment happens before the next condition check
The increment happens first, then the condition is checked, then initialization
The condition is checked before initialization
The increment is unnecessary in MIPS
questions.explanation: For loops follow the pattern: initialize once, then repeatedly check condition, execute body, increment, and loop back. This matches standard control flow semantics.

questions.question:
A programmer writes this MIPS code for a while loop but forgets the branch instruction:

loop: lw $t0, 0($sp)
      addi $t0, $t0, 1
      sw $t0, 0($sp)
      # Missing instruction here

Without the missing branch, what happens?
choices: The code executes only once and continues past the loop
The loop repeats infinitely
The program crashes immediately
The loop executes 10 times by default
questions.explanation: Without a branch instruction (like bne or beq to jump back to the loop label), execution continues sequentially to the next instruction instead of looping, so the loop body executes only once.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS translation of `while (arr[i] != 0) { i++; }` where $t0 = i, $t1 = base address of arr:

loop: sll $t2, $t0, 2
      add $t2, $t1, $t2
      lw $t3, 0($t2)
      beq $t3, $zero, end_loop
      addi $t0, $t0, 1
      j loop
end_loop:

What is the purpose of `sll $t2, $t0, 2`?
choices: To convert the array index to a byte offset (multiply by 4 for word size)
To shift the loop counter left for faster comparison
To allocate space on the stack for the loop
To clear the lower 2 bits of the index
questions.explanation: sll (shift left logical) by 2 multiplies by 4, converting an array index to a byte offset since each word is 4 bytes. This allows proper address calculation for array access.

questions.question: A loop is written as: `for (i = n; i > 0; i--)`. An incorrect MIPS translation uses `slt $t1, $zero, $t0` (instead of `slt $t1, $zero, $t0` after decrement) to check the condition. What goes wrong?
choices: The loop condition is checked before the decrement, causing an off-by-one error where the loop executes one extra time
The loop never executes because slt always returns false
The loop becomes infinite
The comparison uses unsigned instead of signed arithmetic
questions.explanation: Placing the condition check before the decrement means the initial condition is tested against the unmodified value. When i=n, the check passes, but the first iteration uses n before decrementing, causing one extra iteration compared to the intended behavior.

questions.question: What does the MIPS instruction `slt $t0, $t1, $t2` do?
choices: Sets $t0 to 1 if $t1 < $t2 (signed comparison), otherwise 0
Sets $t0 to 1 if $t1 <= $t2 (signed comparison), otherwise 0
Shifts $t1 left by $t2 bits and stores result in $t0
Sets $t0 to the lesser of $t1 and $t2
questions.explanation: The slt instruction performs a signed less-than comparison and sets the destination register to 1 if the condition is true, 0 otherwise. It does not perform a less-than-or-equal comparison, shift operation, or minimum selection.

questions.question: Which instruction would you use to compare a register against an immediate value in MIPS?
choices: slt $t0, $t1, 5
slti $t0, $t1, 5
slt $t0, 5, $t1
cmp $t0, $t1, 5
questions.explanation: The slti instruction is the immediate variant of slt, allowing comparison with a constant value. The slt instruction requires two registers, and cmp is not a valid MIPS instruction.

questions.question: After executing `slti $t3, $t4, 100`, what value will be in $t3 if $t4 contains 50?
questions.explanation: Since 50 < 100 is true, the slti instruction sets $t3 to 1. The actual values being compared are not stored in the destination register; only the boolean result (1 for true) is stored.

questions.question:
Consider this code snippet:
```
addi $t1, $zero, 10
addi $t2, $zero, -5
slt $t0, $t1, $t2
```
What value will be in $t0 after execution?
questions.explanation: The slt instruction compares $t1 (10) with $t2 (-5). Since 10 is not less than -5, the condition is false and $t0 is set to 0. The slt instruction performs signed comparison, so -5 is correctly interpreted as negative.

questions.question: Which of the following code sequences correctly uses slt to implement the conditional branch `if (x < y) goto label`?
choices:
slt $t0, $s0, $s1
bne $t0, $zero, label

slt $t0, $s1, $s0
bne $t0, $zero, label

slti $t0, $s0, $s1
bne $t0, $zero, label

slt $s0, $s1, $zero
bne $s0, $zero, label
questions.explanation: To implement `if (x < y)`, we use slt to compare $s0 (x) and $s1 (y), storing the result in $t0. If the result is 1 (true), we branch. The second option reverses the comparison, and the third uses an immediate with a non-sensical value.

questions.question:
After executing this sequence:
```
addi $t1, $zero, -32768
addi $t2, $zero, -32769
slti $t0, $t1, -32769
```
What is in $t0?
choices: Undefined (overflow)
questions.explanation: The slti instruction compares $t1 (-32768) with the immediate value -32769. Since -32768 is greater than -32769, the condition is false and $t0 is set to 0. Both values are within the valid signed 16-bit range for the immediate.

questions.question: In MIPS, what is the key difference between slt and sltu instructions?
choices: slt works with registers while sltu only works with immediates
slt performs signed comparison while sltu performs unsigned comparison
slt sets the register to the smaller value while sltu sets it to 1 or 0
slt uses two operands while sltu uses three operands
questions.explanation: The slt instruction interprets operands as signed integers, while sltu interprets them as unsigned integers. This affects how negative values are treated in the comparison. Both instructions set the destination to 1 or 0 based on the comparison result.

questions.question: Consider the instruction `slti $t0, $t1, 32767`. What problem might occur if you try to use `slti $t0, $t1, 32768`?
choices: The instruction will cause a segmentation fault
The immediate value 32768 exceeds the 16-bit signed range and cannot be directly represented in the instruction
$t1 will be overwritten with an incorrect value
The comparison will always return 0
questions.explanation: The immediate field in slti is limited to 16 bits and interprets values as signed (-32768 to 32767). The value 32768 cannot fit in this range. The assembler would either reject this or implicitly load the value into a register using a pseudo-instruction.

questions.question:
What would be the result of this code sequence?
```
addi $t1, $zero, -1
slt $t0, $t1, $zero
sltu $t2, $t1, $zero
```
questions.explanation: For slt: -1 (signed) < 0 is true, so $t0 = 1. For sltu: -1 is interpreted as 4294967295 (unsigned 32-bit), which is not less than 0, so $t2 = 0. The difference in signed vs. unsigned interpretation is the key distinction.

questions.question: In MIPS, which instruction is used to call a function and automatically save the return address?
choices: jal
jr
j
beq
questions.explanation: jal (jump and link) both jumps to the function address and saves the return address in $ra (register 31). The other instructions either jump without saving (j), return from a function (jr), or are conditional branches (beq).

questions.question: What is the correct instruction to return from a function to the caller in MIPS?
choices: j $ra
jr $ra
jal $ra
return $ra
questions.explanation: jr $ra (jump register) performs an indirect jump to the address stored in $ra, which is the return address saved by jal. The 'r' in jr indicates it uses a register value, not an immediate address.

questions.question: In MIPS, register $ra is automatically set by which instruction?
choices: li $ra, address
jal function_label
move $ra, $31
sw $ra, 0($sp)
questions.explanation: The jal instruction automatically loads the return address (address of the next instruction after jal) into $ra. No other instruction shown performs this automatic assignment.

questions.question:
Consider the following code snippet:

```
main:
  jal add_numbers
  # line X
  
add_numbers:
  add $v0, $a0, $a1
  jr $ra
```

What address does $ra contain when add_numbers executes jr $ra?
choices: The address of the jal instruction
The address of line X (the instruction after jal)
The address of the add instruction inside add_numbers
The address of the jr $ra instruction
questions.explanation: jal saves the address of the next instruction (the one after jal) into $ra. This allows the function to return to the correct location in the calling code when jr $ra executes.

questions.question:
Trace the execution of this MIPS code:

```
  li $a0, 5
  jal double
  move $a0, $v0  # line A
  
double:
  add $v0, $a0, $a0
  jr $ra
```

What value is in $a0 after the jr $ra instruction returns?
choices: Undefined
questions.explanation: jal double causes $ra to be set to the address of 'line A'. The double function sets $v0 to 10 (5+5), then jr $ra returns to line A, which moves $v0 (10) into $a0.

questions.question: If a function modifies $ra during execution but needs to call another function via jal, what must the function do?
choices: Nothing, $ra is automatically preserved by the CPU
Save $ra to the stack before calling jal, then restore it before returning
Use j instead of jal for nested calls
Copy $ra to another register like $s0 before the second jal
questions.explanation: Since jal overwrites $ra with a new return address, a function that needs to make nested function calls must save $ra to the stack before the nested jal, then restore it before executing its own jr $ra to ensure it returns to its caller.

questions.question:
Consider this buggy MIPS code:

```
func:
  add $v0, $a0, $a1
  jal another_func
  jr $ra
  
another_func:
  sub $v0, $v0, 1
  jr $ra
```

Why will this code not work correctly?
choices: The jr $ra in func will jump to the wrong address because jal overwrote $ra
The sub instruction will corrupt the return value
The jal instruction must use a label, not an address
The add and sub instructions cannot both modify $v0
questions.explanation: When jal another_func executes, it overwrites $ra with the return address pointing to jr $ra in func. However, func then immediately executes jr $ra, jumping to the middle of func instead of returning to the caller. func should save $ra before calling another_func.

questions.question: In a MIPS function, if you need to preserve the value in $ra across multiple function calls, which approach is correct?
choices: Copy $ra to $s0 before each jal, then copy it back
Use the stack to push $ra before nested jals, and pop it before the final jr $ra
Avoid using jal and use j with manual address calculations instead
Declare a global variable to store $ra
questions.explanation: The standard convention is to save $ra (and other caller-saved registers) to the stack upon function entry if the function makes nested calls, then restore before returning. This is the only reliable, convention-following approach.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the jal instruction and the $31 register in MIPS?
choices: $31 is an alias for $ra; jal saves the return address to $31
jal uses $31 internally but the programmer should always use $ra
$ra and $31 are different registers; jal stores to $ra only
jal stores to $31, and $ra is a separate register that must be manually updated
questions.explanation: $31 and $ra are the same register—$ra is the conventional name for register 31. When jal executes, it saves the return address into this register, regardless of whether you refer to it as $ra or $31.

questions.question: In MIPS calling conventions, which registers are used to pass the first four integer arguments to a function?
questions.explanation: $a0-$a3 are the argument registers designated by the MIPS calling convention for passing integer arguments. The other registers serve different purposes: $v0-$v1 are for return values, $s0-$s3 are saved registers, and $t0-$t3 are temporary registers.

questions.question: In MIPS, where should a function place its return value(s)?
choices: $v0 for a single value, or $v0-$v1 for two values
$a0 and $a1
$sp and $fp
$ra and $gp
questions.explanation: The MIPS calling convention specifies that return values go into $v0 (for a single 32-bit value) or $v0-$v1 (for two 32-bit values). The other registers are used for arguments, stack management, and control flow respectively.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly shows how to pass three arguments (10, 20, 30) to a function in MIPS?
questions.explanation: Arguments are passed in $a0, $a1, $a2 (and $a3 for a fourth argument). Using li to load immediate values into these registers is the correct way to prepare arguments before a function call.

questions.question:
Consider this MIPS code:
```
li $a0, 5
li $a1, 3
jal multiply
move $s0, $v0
```
Assuming `multiply` returns the product in $v0, what will be stored in $s0 after execution?
questions.explanation: The function `multiply` is called with arguments 5 and 3 in $a0 and $a1 respectively. It should return their product (15) in $v0, which is then moved into $s0. This traces through the calling convention correctly.

questions.question: A function receives four arguments in $a0-$a3. If the function needs to preserve one of these argument values after making a call to another function, what should it do?
choices: Save the argument value to the stack before calling the other function
Move it to a $t register before calling
Move it to $v0 or $v1
Call the other function with fewer arguments to avoid overwriting
questions.explanation: Argument registers $a0-$a3 are not preserved across function calls and will be overwritten. To preserve a value, it must be saved to the stack or moved to a saved register like $s0-$s7 before making a nested call.

questions.question:
