choices: 4 times
5 times
6 times
25 times
questions.explanation: The function is called for factorial(5), factorial(4), factorial(3), factorial(2), factorial(1), and returns immediately for the base case, totaling 6 function calls including the initial call.

questions.question: An algorithm processes an input of size n by dividing it in half recursively and processing each half independently. Which Big-O notation best describes this algorithm's time complexity?
choices: O(n²)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
O(2ⁿ)
questions.explanation: Dividing the problem in half recursively creates a recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1), which by the Master Theorem gives O(n log n) complexity, representing the cost of processing all levels of recursion.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of establishing a base case in a recursive function?
choices: To maximize the recursion depth
To prevent infinite recursion and provide a termination condition
To increase the time complexity
To reduce the number of parameters
questions.explanation: A base case is essential to stop the recursive chain; without it, the function would call itself indefinitely, causing a stack overflow. It provides the necessary termination condition.

questions.question: Two algorithms have complexities T₁(n) = 3n² + 5n + 2 and T₂(n) = n³ + n. For very large values of n, which statement is true?
choices: T₁(n) will always execute faster
T₂(n) will execute faster because cubic growth dominates quadratic growth
T₁(n) is O(n²) and T₂(n) is O(n³), so T₁(n) is better asymptotically
Both algorithms have identical performance
questions.explanation: Asymptotic analysis focuses on dominant terms for large n; T₁(n) reduces to O(n²) and T₂(n) reduces to O(n³). Since n² grows slower than n³ for large n, T₁(n) performs better asymptotically.

questions.question: A recursive algorithm solves a problem of size n by making 4 recursive calls on subproblems of size n/2, plus O(n) work to combine results. Using the Master Theorem, what is the time complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(4ⁿ)
questions.explanation: The recurrence is T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n). By the Master Theorem with a=4, b=2, and f(n)=n, we compare n with n^(log₂4) = n². Since n < n², the complexity is O(n²).

questions.question: Consider a recursive algorithm that makes a single recursive call on a subproblem of size n-1 with O(n) work per call. Derive the recurrence relation and determine its time complexity.
choices: T(n) = T(n-1) + n, resulting in O(n)
T(n) = T(n-1) + n, resulting in O(n²)
T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n, resulting in O(2ⁿ)
T(n) = T(n/2) + n, resulting in O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + n expands to n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n+1)/2, which simplifies to O(n²). This represents a linear recursion depth with linear work at each level.

questions.question: An algorithm's performance is measured as T(n) = 100n³ + 50n² + 10n + 5. Another algorithm performs at S(n) = n⁴. For n = 1000, which algorithm is asymptotically superior and why?
choices: T(n) because the constant 100 is larger and dominates
S(n) because quartic complexity is always better than cubic regardless of constants
T(n) is asymptotically superior because O(n³) grows slower than O(n⁴) for all sufficiently large n
Both algorithms have equivalent asymptotic behavior since both are polynomial
questions.explanation: Asymptotic analysis considers the dominant term and ignores constants. T(n) is O(n³) while S(n) is O(n⁴); for sufficiently large n, cubic growth will always eventually outperform quartic growth, making T(n) asymptotically superior.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of merge sort in the worst case?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: Merge sort divides the array into halves recursively (log n levels) and merges them back together (n operations per level), resulting in O(n log n) worst-case complexity regardless of input order.

questions.question: Why is quicksort considered more practical than merge sort for in-place sorting of large arrays?
choices: It has better worst-case time complexity
It requires O(1) auxiliary space while merge sort requires O(n)
It works better with linked lists
It is simpler to implement correctly
questions.explanation: Although merge sort has guaranteed O(n log n) complexity, quicksort uses O(log n) space for recursion versus O(n) for merge sort's temporary arrays, making it more memory-efficient for large datasets despite potentially worse worst-case scenarios.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is most suitable for nearly sorted data?
choices: Quicksort
Insertion sort
Merge sort
Heap sort
questions.explanation: Insertion sort performs well on nearly sorted data because it only shifts elements slightly from their final positions, achieving O(n) best-case time complexity when the array is already sorted or nearly sorted.

questions.question: What is a critical disadvantage of using quicksort with a fixed pivot selection strategy (e.g., always choosing the first element)?
choices: It cannot handle duplicate elements
It degrades to O(n²) time complexity on already sorted or reverse-sorted arrays
It requires additional memory for partitioning
It is unstable and changes the relative order of equal elements
questions.explanation: Fixed pivot selection can lead to highly unbalanced partitions on already sorted arrays, causing the algorithm to behave like bubble sort with O(n²) complexity. Randomized or median-of-three pivot selection mitigates this problem.

questions.question: Consider an array of 10,000 elements that is already sorted. You need to add 50 new elements and keep the array sorted. Which approach is most efficient?
choices: Use merge sort on the entire array after adding elements
Use insertion sort to insert each new element into its correct position
Use quicksort with random pivot selection
Use heap sort to rebuild the entire array
questions.explanation: Insertion sort on nearly sorted data (inserting 50 elements into a 10,000-element sorted array) runs in approximately O(10,000 × 50) time, which is more efficient than re-sorting the entire array with O(n log n) algorithms.

questions.question: A sorting algorithm is described as 'stable.' What does this property guarantee about the algorithm's behavior?
choices: The time complexity remains constant regardless of input distribution
Elements with equal keys maintain their relative order from the original array
The algorithm always uses O(log n) space
The algorithm will never access the same element twice
questions.explanation: Stability means that when two elements have equal sort keys, their relative positions from the input array are preserved in the output. This is important when sorting objects with multiple comparable attributes.

questions.question: You are implementing an external sorting algorithm to sort 1 million records that don't fit in memory. Which approach is most appropriate and why?
choices: Use quicksort with the smallest partition size that fits in memory
Use merge sort, dividing the data into chunks that fit in memory, sorting each chunk, then merging the sorted runs
Use insertion sort on streaming data without storing all elements
Use heap sort with a priority queue that reads elements lazily
questions.explanation: Merge sort is optimal for external sorting because it processes data sequentially and minimizes disk I/O by sorting memory-sized chunks independently, then merging the pre-sorted runs in a balanced manner that completes in O(n log k) disk operations where k is the number of chunks.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines an Abstract Data Type (ADT)?
choices: A specification of data and operations with defined behavior, independent of implementation
A concrete implementation of a data structure in a specific programming language
A type of tree that only exists in theoretical computer science
A class that inherits from multiple parent classes
questions.explanation: An ADT defines what operations are available and their expected behavior without specifying how they are implemented. This allows for different implementations to satisfy the same ADT specification.

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree, you perform an in-order traversal and get the sequence: 3, 7, 5, 9, 11. What can you conclude?
choices: The tree is a valid BST
The tree violates the BST property
The tree is perfectly balanced
The root node must be 7
questions.explanation: In-order traversal of a valid BST produces elements in sorted order. Since 7 > 5, this sequence is not sorted, indicating the tree violates the BST property where all left descendants must be smaller than their parent.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using an ADT over a concrete data structure implementation?
choices: ADTs always have better time complexity
ADTs allow you to change implementations without affecting code that uses the data structure
ADTs eliminate the need for algorithms
ADTs automatically optimize memory usage
questions.explanation: ADTs provide abstraction, allowing you to swap implementations (e.g., using different BST variants) without changing client code that depends on the ADT interface.

questions.question: When inserting a new node into a BST, what is the time complexity in the worst case and when does this occur?
choices: O(log n) always, regardless of tree structure
O(n) when the tree is completely unbalanced (essentially a linked list)
O(1) for the first insertion, then O(log n) for others
O(n²) due to tree restructuring
questions.explanation: Insertion requires traversing from root to insertion point. In a balanced tree this is O(log n), but in a skewed tree where all nodes are in a chain, traversal takes O(n) time.

questions.question: Consider a BST with nodes containing values: 50, 25, 75, 12, 37, 62, 87. Which value, when deleted using the two-child deletion strategy, requires finding an in-order successor?
questions.explanation: Node 50 (root) has two children. When deleting a node with two children, we replace it with either the in-order successor (smallest in right subtree = 62) or in-order predecessor. Nodes 12 and 87 have fewer than two children; 25 has two children but any would work for this question.

questions.question: A poorly implemented BST degenerates into a linked list structure. How would you restore balance and what ADT property ensures this doesn't happen automatically?
choices: Use rotations; basic BST ADT doesn't guarantee balance, only ordering
Reinsert all elements; the Queue ADT prevents degradation
Delete and recreate the tree; Stacks maintain balance automatically
Use a hash table instead; BSTs are inherently self-balancing
questions.explanation: Rotations (used in AVL trees and Red-Black trees) restore balance. The basic BST ADT only guarantees the ordering property (left < parent < right), not balance. Balanced variants are separate ADTs with additional invariants.

questions.question: Given a BST where you need to implement a range query (find all nodes with values between x and y), what is the optimal approach and its complexity?
choices: Perform a complete in-order traversal and filter results; O(n) regardless of range size
Use binary search on both boundaries and traverse only the sub-tree between them; O(k + log n) where k is the number of results
Store all values in a sorted array for O(log n) lookup; requires O(n) space overhead
Use hashing to store BST nodes; O(1) per query but loses ordering benefits
questions.explanation: The optimal approach exploits BST ordering by finding the boundaries through binary search (O(log n)) then traversing only the relevant subtree, visiting k nodes in the range plus log n nodes for searching. This is significantly better than examining all n nodes when k is small.

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree, what is the time complexity of finding the in-order successor of a node with two children?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The in-order successor of a node with two children is the leftmost node in its right subtree. In a balanced BST, this operation takes O(log n) time on average. In the worst case of a skewed tree, it could be O(n).

questions.question: Which graph representation uses the least space for a sparse graph with V vertices and E edges?
choices: Adjacency matrix
Adjacency list
Edge list with matrix storage
Incidence matrix
questions.explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space, which is optimal for sparse graphs where E << V². An adjacency matrix always uses O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges.

questions.question: After deleting the root node from a Binary Search Tree where the root has two children, which node should replace it?
choices: The largest node in the left subtree
The smallest node in the right subtree
Either the in-order predecessor or in-order successor
Any leaf node from the tree
questions.explanation: When deleting a node with two children, either the in-order predecessor (largest in left subtree) or in-order successor (smallest in right subtree) can replace it while maintaining BST properties. Both maintain the BST ordering of all remaining nodes.

questions.question: For a directed graph with 5 vertices and 8 edges, what is the size of the adjacency matrix representation?
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices is always a V × V matrix. With 5 vertices, the matrix size is 5 × 5 = 25 cells, regardless of the number of edges.

questions.question: Consider a Binary Search Tree that becomes completely unbalanced (like a linked list). How does this affect the height of the tree and what is the worst-case search complexity?
choices: Height remains O(log n) and search is O(log n)
Height becomes O(n) and search is O(n)
Height becomes O(n) but search remains O(log n)
Height becomes O(n log n) and search is O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a completely skewed BST, the height becomes O(n) as it degenerates into a linked list structure. This directly impacts search complexity, making it O(n) in the worst case as you may need to traverse all n nodes.

questions.question: You have an adjacency list representation of an undirected graph. If you perform a DFS starting from vertex A and mark vertices as visited, what property of the traversal can you exploit to detect a cycle in the graph?
choices: A cycle exists if we visit a vertex that is the parent of the current vertex
A cycle exists if we encounter a visited vertex that is not the immediate parent
A cycle exists if the DFS tree contains back edges to ancestors
A cycle exists only if we revisit the starting vertex A
questions.explanation: In an undirected graph, encountering a visited vertex (other than the immediate parent from which we came) indicates a back edge, which proves a cycle exists. For directed graphs, any visited vertex (including ancestors) indicates a cycle. The correct answer accounts for undirected graphs where we must exclude the parent edge.

questions.question: Given a BST with n nodes where you need to perform m insertions and n lookups, and the tree is initially unbalanced with height O(n), what is the total time complexity of all operations combined?
choices: O(n²)
O(m*n + n²)
O(m*log n + n*log n)
O((m+n)*n)
questions.explanation: With an unbalanced tree of height O(n), each insertion takes O(n) worst-case time, and each lookup takes O(n) worst-case time. Therefore, m insertions take O(m*n) and n lookups take O(n²), giving total O(m*n + n²) = O((m+n)*n) when simplified. This demonstrates why balancing is critical for performance.

questions.question: Which data structure is typically used to implement Depth-First Search (DFS)?
choices: Stack
Queue
Priority Queue
Heap
questions.explanation: DFS uses a stack (either explicit or implicit via recursion) to store vertices and explore paths deeply before backtracking. A queue would implement BFS instead.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of a BFS traversal on a graph with V vertices and E edges?
choices: O(V)
O(E)
O(V + E)
O(V * E)
questions.explanation: BFS visits each vertex once and traverses each edge once, resulting in O(V + E) time complexity. Both vertices and edges must be accounted for in the total time.

questions.question: In a DFS traversal of an undirected graph, which type of edge cannot exist?
choices: Back edge
Forward edge
Cross edge
Tree edge
questions.explanation: In undirected graphs, forward edges do not exist as separate entities because edges are bidirectional. What appears as a forward edge in a directed graph is simply a back edge in the undirected case.

questions.question: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) must have at least one vertex with in-degree 0. Which algorithm can be used to identify such vertices for topological sorting?
choices: DFS with cycle detection
BFS to find all vertices with in-degree 0
Dijkstra's algorithm
Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.explanation: Topological sorting commonly uses Kahn's algorithm, which identifies and processes vertices with in-degree 0 using BFS-like iteration. DFS can also work but BFS with in-degree tracking is more direct for this purpose.

questions.question: When performing DFS on a directed graph, a back edge indicates the existence of a cycle. If during DFS traversal you encounter a vertex that is currently in the recursion stack, what does this signify?
choices: The graph is a tree
A cycle exists in the graph
The vertex is unreachable
The graph is bipartite
questions.explanation: A vertex in the current recursion stack that is revisited indicates a back edge, which proves a cycle exists. This is the key property used for cycle detection in directed graphs.

questions.question: Given an undirected graph where you need to determine if it is bipartite, which traversal approach is most suitable and why?
choices: DFS because it explores deeper paths faster
BFS because it systematically assigns alternating colors level by level
Both DFS and BFS work equally, but BFS is preferred for clarity
Dijkstra's algorithm for shortest path verification
questions.explanation: While both DFS and BFS can detect bipartiteness through 2-coloring, BFS is often preferred because it naturally assigns alternating colors level by level, making the logic more intuitive and easier to verify. Both have the same O(V + E) complexity.

questions.question: In a strongly connected component (SCC) problem on a directed graph, the Kosaraju algorithm performs DFS twice. What is the purpose of the second DFS pass on the transpose graph?
choices: To verify that the graph is acyclic
To assign vertices to their respective SCCs by processing vertices in decreasing order of finish times
To count the total number of edges
To find the shortest path between components
questions.explanation: The second DFS on the transposed graph, processing vertices in decreasing finish time order from the first pass, ensures that each DFS tree in the second pass corresponds to exactly one SCC. This clever ordering guarantees correct identification of all strongly connected components.

questions.question: Which graph representation is most space-efficient for a sparse graph with V vertices and E edges where E << V²?
choices: Adjacency matrix with O(V²) space
Adjacency list with O(V + E) space
Edge list with O(V × E) space
Incidence matrix with O(V × E) space
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists use O(V + E) space, which is optimal for sparse graphs. Adjacency matrices always use O(V²) space regardless of edge count, making them inefficient when E is much smaller than V².

questions.question: What is the key difference between DFS and BFS in terms of the data structure used?
choices: DFS uses a queue while BFS uses a stack
DFS uses a stack while BFS uses a queue
Both use the same data structure but in different orders
DFS uses recursion while BFS requires iteration
questions.explanation: DFS employs a stack (either explicit or through recursion) to explore deeply into branches, while BFS uses a queue to explore level-by-level. This fundamental difference determines the order in which vertices are visited.

questions.question: In a BFS traversal starting from vertex S, a vertex V is discovered at distance 3. If you later encounter V again during traversal from a different parent, why shouldn't you update V's distance?
choices: BFS hasn't visited all vertices yet
The new path cannot be shorter since BFS explores in order of increasing distance
Updating would create a cycle in the graph
The graph must be undirected
questions.explanation: BFS guarantees that when a vertex is first discovered, it has been reached via a shortest path. Since BFS explores vertices in distance order, any subsequent encounter must be from a path of equal or greater length, so the distance shouldn't be updated.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm fails on graphs with negative edge weights. Which of the following best explains why?
choices: Negative weights cause integer overflow
The greedy selection of minimum distance may be invalidated by discovering shorter paths through negative edges later
Negative weights create infinite loops
The algorithm cannot initialize distance values correctly
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach assumes that once a vertex's shortest path is determined, it cannot be improved. Negative edges violate this assumption by allowing paths to become shorter through later vertices, making the greedy selection invalid.

questions.question: For a graph with V vertices and E edges, what is the time complexity of DFS using an adjacency list representation?
choices: O(V²)
O(V + E)
O(E log V)
O(V × E)
questions.explanation: DFS visits each vertex once and examines each edge at most twice (once from each direction in undirected graphs), resulting in O(V + E) time complexity. This is more efficient than O(V²) when the graph is sparse.

questions.question: Consider a weighted directed graph where you need to find shortest paths from a single source to all vertices. The graph contains negative edge weights but no negative cycles. Which algorithm is most appropriate and why?
choices: Dijkstra's because it's always faster
Bellman-Ford because it handles negative weights correctly while Dijkstra's only works with non-negative weights
BFS because it explores all paths equally
Floyd-Warshall because it's a complete algorithm
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford is specifically designed to handle negative edge weights while correctly finding shortest paths, unlike Dijkstra's which relies on greedy selection that fails with negatives. It relaxes edges V-1 times to guarantee optimal paths in acyclic weight scenarios.

questions.question: In an adjacency list representation, you perform DFS on a graph and notice the traversal order differs from another DFS implementation. What could explain this difference without indicating an algorithmic error?
choices: One implementation uses a queue instead of a stack
The order of neighbors in the adjacency list differs between implementations
One graph has a negative cycle that the other doesn't
The starting vertex must be different
questions.explanation: DFS correctness doesn't depend on the specific traversal order—different orderings of neighbors in adjacency lists will produce different valid DFS traversals. Both are correct as long as they follow the DFS principle of exploring deeply before backtracking, making implementation-specific neighbor ordering a valid source of variation.

questions.question: In a directed weighted graph, what is the key requirement for Dijkstra's algorithm to produce correct results?
choices: All edge weights must be non-negative
The graph must be connected
The graph must be acyclic
All vertices must have equal degree
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm relies on the greedy property that once a vertex's shortest distance is determined, it won't be improved. Negative weights violate this assumption, potentially causing incorrect results.

questions.question: Consider a weighted directed graph with vertices A, B, C, D. Starting from A, which data structure is most efficient for Dijkstra's algorithm to extract the minimum distance vertex repeatedly?
choices: Unsorted array
Min-heap or priority queue
Hash table
Balanced binary search tree
questions.explanation: A min-heap or priority queue allows O(log V) extraction of the minimum distance vertex, making the overall algorithm O((V+E) log V). An unsorted array would require O(V) for each extraction.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms for finding minimum spanning trees?
choices: Kruskal's works only on directed graphs while Prim's works on undirected graphs
Kruskal's builds the MST edge-by-edge by sorting edges globally, while Prim's grows the tree vertex-by-vertex from a starting vertex
Prim's algorithm has better time complexity in all cases
Kruskal's requires the graph to be connected, but Prim's does not
questions.explanation: Kruskal's sorts all edges and adds them greedily without creating cycles (using union-find). Prim's starts from a vertex and repeatedly adds the minimum weight edge connecting the tree to an unvisited vertex. Both work on undirected weighted graphs and require connectivity.

questions.question: In a weighted directed graph with n vertices and m edges, if you run Dijkstra's algorithm using an adjacency list and binary heap, what is the time complexity?
choices: O(n²)
O(n log n + m)
O((n + m) log n)
O(m² log n)
questions.explanation: With a binary heap, each vertex is extracted O(n) times (O(n log n) total) and each edge is relaxed once (O(m log n) total for heap operations). The combined complexity is O((n + m) log n).

questions.question: A minimum spanning tree of a connected weighted graph with 8 vertices must have exactly how many edges?
choices: 7 edges
8 edges
At least 14 edges
It depends on the edge weights
questions.explanation: An MST connects all n vertices with exactly n-1 edges, forming a tree. For 8 vertices, this is always 7 edges regardless of the specific graph structure or weights.

questions.question: You have a weighted directed graph where Dijkstra's algorithm produces shortest paths from source vertex S. If you add a positive constant k to every edge weight, how does this affect the shortest path tree from S?
choices: The shortest path tree remains identical
The shortest path tree will definitely change to a different set of edges
It depends on the structure of the graph and whether paths have different lengths
All paths will have equal cost, making any spanning tree valid
questions.explanation: Adding a constant k to all edges is equivalent to adding k × (path length) to each path's total cost. Since this adds the same multiplicative factor to all paths of the same length, the relative ordering is preserved and the shortest path tree remains unchanged.

questions.question: In Prim's algorithm for MSTs, you maintain a priority queue of edges. At each iteration, when you add a new vertex v to the tree, what must you do with edges incident to v?
choices: Remove all edges incident to v from the priority queue
Add all edges from v to unvisited vertices to the priority queue, updating priorities as needed
Sort all edges incident to v and process them immediately
Ignore edges incident to v until all other vertices are processed
questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm greedily grows the MST by always selecting the minimum weight edge connecting a visited vertex to an unvisited vertex. When a new vertex is added, all its incident edges to unvisited vertices become candidates for the next iteration.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a hash function in a hash table?
choices: To map keys to array indices in a deterministic and uniform manner
To encrypt sensitive data for security purposes
To sort the keys in ascending order
To reduce memory usage by compressing keys
questions.explanation: A hash function converts keys into array indices deterministically and aims for uniform distribution to minimize collisions. It is not designed for encryption, sorting, or compression of keys.

questions.question: A hash table has 10 slots and currently stores 8 elements. What is the load factor?
questions.explanation: Load factor is calculated as (number of elements) / (number of slots), which is 8/10 = 0.8. This indicates the hash table is 80% full and may warrant resizing depending on the collision resolution strategy.

questions.question: In open addressing with linear probing, if a collision occurs at index i, where is the next position checked?
choices: At index (i + hash(key)) mod m
At index (i + 1) mod m
At a random index in the table
At the end of the hash table
questions.explanation: Linear probing checks the next consecutive index (i + 1) mod m when a collision occurs. This simple approach is easy to implement but can cause clustering, reducing performance over time.

questions.question: Which collision resolution technique typically has better cache locality and is suitable for hardware optimization?
choices: Separate chaining with linked lists
Open addressing with linear probing
Double hashing with prime numbers
Cuckoo hashing with multiple tables
questions.explanation: Open addressing with linear probing keeps data in contiguous array slots, improving CPU cache locality compared to separate chaining which uses pointers and scattered memory locations. This makes it favorable for hardware optimization and sequential access patterns.

questions.question: A hash table using separate chaining has 5 collisions and 20 total insertions. If the table size is 4, what is the average chain length?
questions.explanation: With 20 insertions distributed among 4 slots, the average chain length is 20/4 = 5. However, the question asks about the average given the collision information; with 20 total items and 4 slots, average chain length is simply 20/4 = 5 elements per slot on average, but considering the structure: (20 insertions) / (4 slots) = 5 per slot, or load factor perspective gives us 5/4 = 1.25 as the load factor which relates to average chain length metric.

questions.question: Consider a hash table that uses quadratic probing with hash function h(k) = k mod m. If m = 7 and we insert key k = 15, then encounter a collision, which index should we probe next?
choices: Index 2
Index 3
Index 6
Index 4
questions.explanation: h(15) = 15 mod 7 = 1. On first collision, quadratic probing checks h(15) + 1² = 1 + 1 = 2. If still occupied, it checks h(15) + 2² = 1 + 4 = 5, then h(15) + 3² = 1 + 9 mod 7 = 3, then h(15) + 4² = 1 + 16 mod 7 = 3 + 2 = 5... The sequence of quadratic probing offsets (1, 4, 9, 16, ...) modulo 7 generates specific positions; after checking position 2 (offset 1²), we next check 1 + 4 = 5, then 1 + 9 = 10 mod 7 = 3, and continuing the pattern 1 + 16 mod 7 = 17 mod 7 = 3, 1 + 25 mod 7 = 26 mod 7 = 5, 1 + 36 mod 7 = 37 mod 7 = 2, 1 + 49 mod 7 = 50 mod 7 = 1 back to start; so the answer requires checking the second probe position carefully: (1 + 4) mod 7 = 5, then (1 + 9) mod 7 = 3, then (1 + 16) mod 7 = 3 again... Following quadratic sequence more carefully with offset i²: probes at 1, (1+1) mod 7 = 2, (1+4) mod 7 = 5, (1+9) mod 7 = 3, (1+16) mod 7 = 3, (1+25) mod 7 = 5, (1+36) mod 7 = 2, showing index 6 cannot be reached in this specific pattern without recalculation—verify: examining options and quadratic offset pattern, index 6 would require 1 + offset ≡ 6 (mod 7), so offset ≡ 5 (mod 7), which isn't a perfect square offset in standard quadratic probing.

questions.question: A hash table implementation must choose between separate chaining and open addressing. The application requires very frequent deletions and dynamic key updates. Which approach is more suitable and why?
choices: Open addressing because it uses less memory overhead
Separate chaining because deletions are straightforward without causing probe sequence issues
Open addressing because it has better cache performance
Separate chaining because it has O(1) average insertion time
questions.explanation: Separate chaining is more suitable for frequent deletions because removing an element from a chain is a simple linked list operation. Open addressing complicates deletions because removing an element breaks the probe sequence for other keys, requiring either lazy deletion or full table rehashing. While open addressing has memory and cache advantages, correctness for deletions favors chaining.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of extracting the minimum element from a min-heap containing n elements?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Extracting the root (minimum) is O(1), but the subsequent heapify operation to restore the heap property requires O(log n) comparisons and swaps along the height of the tree.

questions.question: In a binary max-heap represented as an array, if a node is at index i, what is the index of its parent?
questions.explanation: The parent of a node at index i in a 0-indexed array is always at index (i-1)/2. This relationship holds for both children at 2*i+1 and 2*i+2.

questions.question: When building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the bottom-up heapify approach, what is the overall time complexity?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
questions.explanation: Although heapify is O(log n), building from bottom-up processes nodes level by level, with most nodes near leaves requiring minimal heapify work. The total cost sums to O(n), not O(n log n).

questions.question: A trie node for alphabet strings typically contains pointers to child nodes and a boolean flag. What is the boolean flag used for?
choices: To mark nodes visited during traversal
To indicate if the node represents the end of a valid word
To track parent pointers for deletion
To balance the tree structure
questions.explanation: The boolean flag (often called isEndOfWord) marks whether a path from root to this node completes a valid string. This distinguishes actual words from intermediate nodes on paths to longer words.

questions.question: In a priority queue implemented with a binary min-heap, after removing the minimum element and calling heapify, which property guarantees the operation completes in O(log n)?
choices: The array must be sorted
The heap property is maintained at every level
All leaf nodes are at the same depth
The tree is perfectly balanced
questions.explanation: The heap property (parent ≤ children for min-heap) is maintained throughout heapify operations. Since the tree is complete with height O(log n), at most O(log n) comparisons occur down the height.

questions.question: Consider inserting the sequence [15, 10, 20, 8, 2] into an initially empty min-heap. After all insertions, what is the root value and what operation ensures it remains valid?
choices: Root is 15; bubble-down maintains heap property
Root is 2; bubble-up maintains heap property
Root is 2; bubble-down maintains heap property
Root is 8; insert-balancing maintains heap property
questions.explanation: After inserting all elements, the minimum value 2 becomes the root. Each insertion uses bubble-up, but the final heap structure has 2 at the root, verified by bubble-down properties. The root is always the minimum in a min-heap.

questions.question: A trie-based autocomplete system stores m words with average length k. When searching for all completions of a prefix of length p, what is the time complexity, and what is the primary factor limiting performance?
choices: O(k*m); searching all m words in the trie
O(p + n); where n is the number of words with that prefix
O(p*k); searching through all trie levels
O(m log m); sorting matching completions
questions.explanation: Finding the prefix node takes O(p) time. From that node, a DFS/BFS collects all complete words below it in O(n) time, where n is the number of matching words. Total is O(p + n), making it efficient for large vocabularies with selective prefixes.

questions.question: Which of the following algorithms has the best average-case time complexity for sorting an unsorted array of n elements?
choices: Bubble sort: O(n²)
Merge sort: O(n log n)
Quick sort: O(n log n)
Selection sort: O(n²)
questions.explanation: Quick sort has an average-case time complexity of O(n log n), making it more efficient than bubble sort and selection sort which are O(n²). While merge sort also achieves O(n log n), quick sort is typically faster in practice due to better cache locality and lower space requirements.

questions.question: In a hash table with open addressing and linear probing, what is the primary disadvantage compared to separate chaining?
choices: It requires more memory for pointers
It is susceptible to clustering, reducing search efficiency
It cannot handle negative hash values
It always has O(1) insertion time
questions.explanation: Linear probing in open addressing suffers from primary clustering, where consecutive occupied slots form clusters, increasing the average number of probes needed for insertion and lookup. This degrades performance as the load factor increases, unlike separate chaining which maintains independent linked lists.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two nodes in a balanced binary search tree?
choices: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In a balanced BST, finding the LCA requires traversing from the root downward, following the binary search property. Since the tree is balanced with height O(log n), the search path is at most O(log n) nodes, giving O(log n) time complexity.

questions.question: Consider an algorithm that uses dynamic programming to solve the 0/1 knapsack problem with n items and capacity W. How does the space complexity improve using the 1D array optimization compared to the 2D table approach?
choices: From O(W) to O(n)
From O(nW) to O(W)
From O(n²) to O(n)
From O(nW) to O(n²)
questions.explanation: The standard 2D DP table requires O(nW) space to store dp[i][j] values. The space-optimized version uses only a 1D array of size W, since each new row depends only on the previous row. This reduces space complexity from O(nW) to O(W) while maintaining the same O(nW) time complexity.

questions.question: Which graph traversal algorithm is most appropriate for finding the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph?
choices: Depth-first search with backtracking
Breadth-first search
Dijkstra's algorithm
Prim's algorithm
questions.explanation: Breadth-first search explores nodes level by level, guaranteeing that the first path found to any node is the shortest path in an unweighted graph. DFS doesn't guarantee shortest paths, Dijkstra's is unnecessary for unweighted graphs, and Prim's is for minimum spanning trees, not shortest paths.

questions.question: You have a sorted array of n distinct integers and need to find if a target value exists using only comparisons. An algorithm checks the middle element, then recursively searches the appropriate half. Prove that this requires at most ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ comparisons and explain why no comparison-based algorithm can do better.
choices: Binary search is optimal because the information-theoretic lower bound for n possibilities requires log₂(n) comparisons, and binary search achieves ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉
Linear search is actually faster in practice despite worse complexity
Any divide-and-conquer strategy automatically achieves the optimal bound
The bound is tight only when n is a power of 2 minus 1
questions.explanation: Binary search achieves the information-theoretic lower bound because each comparison eliminates roughly half the remaining possibilities. Since there are n+1 possible outcomes (element found or not found, and where), any decision tree must have depth at least ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉. Binary search matches this bound, proving optimality for comparison-based search.

questions.question: A weighted directed graph has edges with both positive and negative weights but no negative cycles. You need single-source shortest paths from vertex s. Why is Dijkstra's algorithm unsuitable, and what is the best choice considering the constraint?
choices: Dijkstra fails because it's too slow; use Bellman-Ford which runs in O(VE)
Dijkstra fails on negative edges; use Bellman-Ford which handles negatives and detects negative cycles in O(VE)
Dijkstra works fine; the concern about negative weights is a common misconception
Use DFS with dynamic programming memoization to avoid revisiting vertices
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy strategy assumes that once a vertex is finalized, no shorter path exists to it—an assumption violated by negative edges. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times, correctly handling negative weights. Since there are no negative cycles, it finds optimal paths in O(VE) time and can detect negative cycles in the V-th iteration.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why software often fails in production despite passing internal testing?
choices: Testing environments rarely replicate real-world usage patterns, hardware configurations, and user behaviors
Software developers intentionally introduce bugs to justify future maintenance work
Production failures only occur when users deliberately misuse the software
Testing is performed too early in the development cycle to catch any defects
questions.explanation: Production failures occur when the testing environment differs from actual deployment conditions in terms of data volume, hardware, concurrent users, and usage patterns. Controlled testing environments cannot anticipate all possible real-world scenarios.

questions.question: During the requirements phase of a project, a team discovers that the documented requirements contradict the stakeholder's actual business needs. Which quality assurance concept does this scenario best illustrate?
choices: A verification failure, because the requirements document was not properly reviewed
A validation failure, because the team is building a solution that doesn't meet actual user needs
A deployment issue that cannot be resolved through testing
A management failure unrelated to software quality
questions.explanation: Validation ensures that the right product is being built to satisfy actual user needs. This scenario represents a validation problem where the requirements themselves fail to capture what users truly need, regardless of how well the software implements those requirements.

questions.question: In the V-model, at which development phase would you expect to design the acceptance test cases?
choices: During the coding phase, when developers understand the implementation details
During the requirements phase, in parallel with high-level requirement documentation
Only after all development is complete, before deployment
Continuously throughout development without a specific phase
questions.explanation: The V-model shows that acceptance test design aligns with the requirements phase on the left side of the V. This ensures tests are designed based on what stakeholders require before implementation begins, allowing for early validation planning.

questions.question: A software team implements a feature exactly as specified in the design document, and unit tests confirm the code works correctly. However, when integrated with other modules, the feature causes system failures. What does this primarily indicate?
choices: The unit tests were inadequate and developers should have written more of them
Verification succeeded (building the product right) but integration issues reveal validation concerns
The design document was written by someone without programming experience
The feature should never have been developed in the first place
questions.explanation: This scenario demonstrates successful verification at the module level but reveals integration and systemic issues. While each component is built correctly per specifications, the overall system doesn't function properly, indicating a validation problem where the integrated solution fails to meet quality and reliability requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a fundamental cause of software failure that occurs before any code is written?
choices: Inefficient algorithms selected during implementation
Ambiguous, incomplete, or incorrect requirements captured during the planning phase
Poor test case coverage identified after deployment
Inadequate hardware resources during system testing
questions.explanation: Problems in requirements gathering and definition represent upstream causes of failure that propagate through the entire development lifecycle. Errors in this phase are often the most costly to fix because they affect design, development, and testing downstream.

questions.question: Consider a V-model applied to a critical healthcare software system. A team completed comprehensive unit testing and integration testing but discovered during system testing that the software cannot handle required regulatory compliance checks. How should this gap be characterized, and at which model stage should it ideally have been caught?
choices: A verification failure that should have been caught during unit testing with better code reviews
A validation gap that should have been identified during requirements and system design phases, preventing costly late-stage rework
An unavoidable issue since regulatory requirements are unpredictable and cannot be tested in advance
A testing infrastructure problem unrelated to the V-model approach
questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements are known and should be documented in the requirements phase (left side of V). System testing (right side of V) validates against these requirements. This represents a validation failure where either requirements weren't captured or system design didn't address them, causing expensive late discovery.

questions.question: A software product passes all verification activities (code reviews, unit tests, integration tests against specifications) but fails in production because users cannot accomplish their intended tasks efficiently due to poor interface design. Which statement best captures this situation?
choices: The V-model was applied incorrectly because verification should have caught this design flaw
This represents successful verification but validation failure, suggesting the original requirements did not adequately capture usability needs or the design failed to implement them
Users are using the software incorrectly and this is not a software quality issue
The testing phase occurred too late; this problem could only be prevented through agile development practices
questions.explanation: The software met its specifications (verification success) but failed to meet actual user needs (validation failure). This indicates that usability requirements were either missing from the original specification or the design implementation didn't adequately address them, demonstrating the critical distinction between building the product right versus building the right product.

questions.question: For a system accepting ages from 18 to 65, which set of boundary value test cases is most appropriate?
choices: Test 18, 41.5 (midpoint), 65
questions.explanation: Boundary value analysis requires testing at the boundaries (18, 65) and just outside them (17, 66), plus values just inside (19, 64). This catches off-by-one errors and boundary condition bugs that are common sources of defects.

questions.question: When partitioning test inputs into equivalence classes, what is the primary goal?
choices: To maximize the total number of test cases created
To group inputs where one representative test case is sufficient to validate the entire class
To ensure every possible input value is tested individually
To identify which test cases should be automated
questions.explanation: Equivalence partitioning reduces testing effort by recognizing that inputs within the same class should behave identically, so testing one representative value covers the entire class. This maintains effectiveness while reducing test case volume.

questions.question: A decision table for a loan approval system has 4 conditions (income > $50k, credit score > 700, debt ratio < 50%, employment > 2 years). How many combinations must be analyzed before simplification?
choices: 4 combinations
8 combinations
16 combinations
32 combinations
questions.explanation: With 4 independent boolean conditions, the total number of possible combinations is 2^4 = 16. A decision table must initially consider all these combinations to identify which are valid, impossible, or can be consolidated.

questions.question: In cause-effect graphing, what do the intermediate nodes represent?
choices: Test case identifiers
Input conditions and their logical combinations
Expected outputs only
The order in which tests should be executed
questions.explanation: Cause-effect graphs use intermediate nodes to represent AND, OR, and NOT logical operators that combine basic causes (inputs) to determine effects (outputs). These nodes show the logical relationships between conditions.

questions.question: A web form accepts usernames of length 3-20 characters. Using both boundary value and equivalence class analysis, what are the critical test cases?
choices: Test a 2-char name, 3-char name, 10-char name, 20-char name, 21-char name
Test any name between 3-20 characters only
Test 1-char, 3-char, 20-char, 100-char names
Test 3-char and 20-char names only
questions.explanation: This approach combines both techniques: equivalence classes (valid: 3-20 chars, invalid: <3 and >20) with boundary values (just below, at, and just beyond limits). Testing 2-char and 21-char ensures boundary enforcement while 10-char represents the valid class.

questions.question: A system's decision table reveals that certain condition combinations are impossible (infeasible) in the business logic. What should a tester do?
choices: Create test cases for infeasible combinations anyway to find hidden bugs
Remove these combinations from the decision table and document the business rule that makes them impossible
Test half the infeasible combinations as a compromise
Assume the code prevents these combinations and skip testing entirely
questions.explanation: Identifying infeasible combinations is a critical outcome of decision table analysis. These should be documented to clarify business rules and dependencies, then excluded from testing to focus on realistic scenarios. Removing them makes the decision table cleaner and test cases more meaningful.

questions.question: For a temperature control system: when (temperature < 15°C AND mode = heating) OR (temperature > 30°C AND mode = cooling), the system triggers an alert. Using cause-effect graphing, which test scenario most rigorously validates this logic?
choices: Test temperature = 14°C with heating mode only
Test temperature = 31°C with cooling mode only
Test all four boundary conditions: 14°C + heating, 15°C + heating, 30°C + cooling, 31°C + cooling, plus invalid combinations like 14°C + cooling
Test one valid scenario and assume the OR logic works
questions.explanation: Rigorous cause-effect testing requires validating each cause-effect pair at boundaries, testing the OR operator with multiple true conditions, and including invalid combinations to verify the system doesn't trigger false alerts. This comprehensive approach catches logic errors in compound conditions.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of pairwise testing over exhaustive testing?
choices: It reduces the number of test cases needed while maintaining reasonable fault detection capability
It guarantees 100% code coverage of all branches
It eliminates the need for manual test design
It can only be applied to web-based applications
questions.explanation: Pairwise testing significantly reduces test case count by covering all pairs of parameter values rather than all combinations, making it practical for systems with many parameters while still catching most faults.

questions.question: Consider a function with 3 parameters, each having 4 possible values. How many test cases would be needed for complete exhaustive testing versus pairwise testing (approximately)?
choices: Exhaustive: 12, Pairwise: 64
Exhaustive: 64, Pairwise: 16
Exhaustive: 256, Pairwise: 9-16
Exhaustive: 4, Pairwise: 3
questions.explanation: Exhaustive testing requires 4³ = 64 cases, but the question asks for 3×4 = 12... Actually, 4×4×4 = 64 total combinations. Pairwise testing can cover all pairs with roughly 9-16 carefully selected test cases, demonstrating significant reduction.

questions.question: What is the key difference between statement coverage and branch coverage?
choices: Statement coverage is more comprehensive and always achieves higher percentages than branch coverage
Branch coverage requires executing both true and false outcomes of conditional statements, while statement coverage only requires executing each line of code
They are identical metrics with different names
Branch coverage only applies to loops, while statement coverage applies to all code
questions.explanation: Statement coverage simply requires executing each line, but branch coverage requires testing both paths of conditional statements (if/else, loops). A test suite can achieve 100% statement coverage without 100% branch coverage by not executing all branches.

questions.question: For the condition (A && B), what is the minimum number of test cases needed to achieve MC/DC coverage?
choices: 1 test case
2 test cases
3 test cases
4 test cases
questions.explanation: MC/DC requires that each condition independently affects the decision outcome. For (A && B), you need: Case 1: A=T, B=T (result=T), Case 2: A=T, B=F (result=F) to show B's independence, Case 3: A=F, B=T (result=F) to show A's independence. Three test cases achieve MC/DC coverage.

questions.question: A test suite achieves 85% statement coverage but only 60% branch coverage. What does this indicate about the test suite?
choices: The test suite is poorly designed and should be discarded entirely
The test suite executes most statements but fails to exercise many conditional branches, potentially missing defects in decision logic
The test suite has a bug in how coverage is calculated
Branch coverage is incorrectly measured and should be ignored
questions.explanation: This scenario is typical and indicates that while most code lines are executed, many conditional branches (especially false conditions or alternative paths) are not tested. The test suite is weak in exercising decision logic and may miss defects related to branch conditions.

questions.question: When designing a pairwise test suite for a system with 5 parameters (each with 3 values), a tester generates 12 test cases. A colleague argues that 12 cases cannot possibly cover all pairs. What would be the most appropriate response?
choices: The colleague is correct; you need at least 25 test cases for 5 parameters
The colleague is incorrect; 12 carefully selected test cases can cover all pairs through orthogonal array design, even though theoretically 9 pairs exist per parameter
The colleague is partially correct; you need exactly 15 test cases to guarantee pair coverage
The question cannot be answered without knowing the specific pairwise testing tool used
questions.explanation: Using orthogonal arrays and combinatorial design techniques, it is possible to cover all parameter pairs with fewer test cases than naive assumptions suggest. With 5 parameters of 3 values each, 12 test cases can be efficiently designed to cover all pairs while respecting mathematical combinatorial properties.

questions.question: For a complex decision statement: (A || B) && (C || D), determine what MC/DC coverage requires and explain why it is stricter than branch coverage.
choices: MC/DC requires 4 test cases; branch coverage only requires 2, because MC/DC mandates each atomic condition independently affects the final outcome
MC/DC requires 8 test cases; branch coverage requires 4, because MC/DC tests all possible value combinations exhaustively
MC/DC requires 6 test cases; branch coverage requires 3, because MC/DC focuses on individual condition impact while branch coverage only tests decision outcomes
MC/DC and branch coverage are equivalent for compound conditions with multiple operators
questions.explanation: MC/DC is stricter than branch coverage because it requires each condition (A, B, C, D) to independently affect the final decision outcome. Branch coverage only requires testing true/false of the overall decision. For (A || B) && (C || D), MC/DC demands carefully selected test cases ensuring each condition's change independently flips the result, requiring more test cases than simple branch coverage.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of test cases required to achieve basis path coverage for a program with a cyclomatic complexity of 5?
choices: At least 5 independent paths
At least 10 test cases
Exactly 3 test cases
At least 8 independent paths
questions.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity indicates the number of linearly independent paths through a program. Therefore, achieving basis path coverage requires at least M test cases, where M is the cyclomatic complexity value.

questions.question: In data-flow testing, which of the following represents an anomaly that should be detected?
choices: A variable that is defined multiple times in sequence
A variable that is defined but never used (du-anomaly)
A variable that is used immediately after declaration
A variable that appears in multiple functions
questions.explanation: Data-flow anomalies include definitions without uses (du-anomalies), uses without prior definitions, and undefined variable references. A variable defined but never used represents wasted computation and potential logic errors.

questions.question: Consider a program with two nested if-statements and one switch statement with 4 cases. What is the cyclomatic complexity?
questions.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity M = E - N + 2P, where E=edges, N=nodes, P=components. Alternatively, M = 1 + (decision points). Two if-statements add 2 to complexity, and a switch with 4 cases adds 3 (one for each additional case path). Total: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

questions.question: Which metric is most directly related to the minimum number of test cases needed to achieve basis path coverage?
choices: Lines of code (LOC)
Cyclomatic complexity (V)
Afferent coupling
Code duplication percentage
questions.explanation: Cyclomatic complexity directly determines the number of linearly independent paths and thus the minimum test cases required for basis path coverage. LOC is unrelated, coupling measures dependencies, and duplication measures redundancy.

questions.question: A du-path (definition-use path) in data-flow testing is best described as:
choices: Any path from program entry to exit
A path from a variable definition to a use of that variable where no other definition of that variable occurs on the path
A path that exercises all decision branches
A path that minimizes cyclomatic complexity
questions.explanation: A du-path traces the flow from where a variable is defined to where it is used without intervening redefinitions. This is fundamental to data-flow coverage criteria like all-defs, all-uses, and all-du-paths.

questions.question: Given a program module with cyclomatic complexity of 8, afferent coupling of 3, and efferent coupling of 7, which statement is most accurate regarding testing effort?
choices: Testing effort is low because afferent coupling is less than 8
Testing effort is highest due to the high cyclomatic complexity requiring many independent test paths, combined with high external dependencies making isolation difficult
Testing effort depends only on LOC, not on complexity metrics
Efferent coupling has no impact on test case design or difficulty
questions.explanation: High cyclomatic complexity (8) requires more test cases for basis path coverage. High efferent coupling (7) indicates many external dependencies that complicate testing and require mocking/stubbing. Together, these factors significantly increase testing effort and complexity.

questions.question: In analyzing a legacy codebase, you discover a function with cyclomatic complexity of 15 and multiple data-flow anomalies including unused variable definitions. Which refactoring approach best addresses the testing concerns?
choices: Increase test coverage percentage to 100% without changing the code
Extract independent decision logic into separate functions to reduce complexity, and eliminate dead code to resolve data-flow anomalies
Add more logging statements to track variable usage
Merge the function with related functions to reduce the number of functions
questions.explanation: Extracting logic reduces cyclomatic complexity to lower the number of required test paths, making testing more manageable. Removing unused definitions eliminates data-flow anomalies and improves code quality. This addresses root causes rather than symptoms, following principles of sustainable testing and maintainability.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary goal of unit testing?
choices: To verify that individual components work correctly in isolation
To test the entire application as a single integrated system
To identify performance bottlenecks in production
To replace the need for manual testing entirely
questions.explanation: Unit testing focuses on testing individual software units (functions, methods, classes) in isolation to ensure they behave correctly. This allows developers to catch bugs early and verify component logic before integration.

questions.question: In test scaffolding, what is the primary purpose of using a mock object?
choices: To replace expensive or unavailable real objects and verify interactions with them
To increase the execution speed of all unit tests
To eliminate the need for writing actual implementation code
To automatically generate test cases for uncovered code paths
questions.explanation: Mock objects are used to simulate external dependencies that may be costly, unavailable, or not yet implemented. They allow verification of how the unit under test interacts with these dependencies without relying on the real implementations.

questions.question: Consider a scenario where you have a UserService that depends on a DatabaseConnection. Which test scaffolding approach would best allow you to test UserService logic without requiring an actual database?
choices: Create a real DatabaseConnection instance and connect to a production database
Use a mock or stub DatabaseConnection that returns predetermined values
Remove the DatabaseConnection dependency entirely from UserService
Skip testing UserService until the database is fully implemented
questions.explanation: Using a mock or stub allows you to isolate UserService and test its logic independently. The mock DatabaseConnection can return controlled test data, enabling thorough testing without database overhead or external dependencies.

questions.question: A development team is implementing integration testing for a three-tier web application (presentation, business logic, database layers). Which integration testing strategy would be most appropriate if the database layer is not yet complete?
choices: Big-bang integration testing, combining all components simultaneously
Top-down integration testing, starting with presentation layer and mocking lower layers
Sandwich integration testing to test middle layers independently
Performance testing to identify which layer is causing delays
questions.explanation: Top-down integration testing allows you to start testing from the presentation layer while mocking the incomplete database layer. This approach enables parallel development and testing, reducing bottlenecks when dependencies are unavailable.

questions.question: When writing a unit test for a calculateTax() method, you use an assertion that fails unexpectedly. The method receives a Decimal parameter and should return a Decimal. What is the most likely issue preventing proper test execution?
choices: The test framework does not support Decimal type assertions
The calculateTax() method has floating-point precision issues that cause assertion comparison failures
The unit test is missing proper test scaffolding with mocks
Integration tests should be used instead of unit tests for this scenario
questions.explanation: Floating-point and decimal arithmetic often introduce precision errors in comparisons. Unit tests for such methods typically need to use approximate equality assertions (tolerance ranges) rather than exact equality to handle these precision issues reliably.

questions.question: In a complex integration testing scenario, you need to test the interaction between a PaymentProcessor and an ExternalPaymentGateway service. The external service has rate limiting, intermittent failures, and costs money per request. How would you design this test to be reliable and maintainable?
choices: Call the real ExternalPaymentGateway directly in all integration tests
Use a spy object to track real calls while recording and replaying responses in subsequent tests
Create a mock ExternalPaymentGateway for unit tests and use contract testing for actual integration validation
Only test PaymentProcessor in isolation with no reference to the external service
questions.explanation: Contract testing and mocking separate concerns effectively: unit tests use mocks to verify PaymentProcessor logic independently, while contract tests with a test double ensure the integration contract remains valid. This avoids repeated expensive external calls while maintaining integration confidence.

questions.question: A team uses bottom-up integration testing for a system with interdependent modules (Module A depends on B, B depends on C). When Module C contains a critical bug, what advantage does bottom-up integration reveal compared to big-bang testing?
choices: It detects the bug earlier because lower layers are tested first before integration with upper layers
It completely eliminates the need for unit testing of individual modules
It requires fewer test cases overall compared to other integration strategies
It automatically fixes critical bugs before they propagate to upper modules
questions.explanation: Bottom-up integration tests lower-level modules (C) before combining them with dependent modules (B, then A). This approach identifies bugs in foundational components early, preventing defects from propagating through the integration chain, making them easier to isolate and fix.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the primary goal of system testing?
choices: To verify that the entire integrated system meets specified requirements and functions correctly
To identify syntax errors in the source code
To test individual functions in isolation
To measure code coverage percentage
questions.explanation: System testing focuses on the complete, integrated system and its behavior as a whole, ensuring end-to-end functionality against requirements. Unit and component testing address individual elements, while coverage metrics are secondary concerns.

questions.question: In model-based testing, what is the primary role of a formal model?
choices: To replace all manual testing activities
To generate test cases automatically and ensure systematic coverage of system behavior
To document the system architecture
To predict future software failures
questions.explanation: Formal models enable systematic generation of test cases by representing system states and transitions, ensuring comprehensive coverage. Models serve as specifications for test case derivation rather than replacements for testing or predictive tools.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a non-functional testing type?
choices: Performance testing
Security testing
Login functionality testing
Usability testing
questions.explanation: Login functionality testing is a functional test that verifies a specific feature works correctly. Performance, security, and usability are non-functional attributes that describe how well the system operates rather than what specific functions it performs.

questions.question: What is the test oracle problem, and why is it significant in software testing?
choices: It refers to the high cost of test automation frameworks
It is the difficulty in determining whether test outputs are correct when expected results are unknown or hard to define
It describes the problem of scheduling test execution
It refers to insufficient test coverage metrics
questions.explanation: The test oracle problem is a fundamental challenge where testers cannot reliably determine if test results are correct, especially for non-deterministic or complex systems. This makes it difficult to automate testing and validate outcomes objectively.

questions.question: A banking system undergoes system integration testing. The test team discovers that the transaction processing module works correctly in isolation but fails when integrated with the reporting module. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The transaction processing module has a logic error
Integration defects, such as incorrect data format conversion or timing issues between modules
The reporting module is missing required functionality
The test cases are poorly designed
questions.explanation: System integration testing reveals defects that emerge from module interactions, such as incompatible interfaces, incorrect data handling, or timing problems. A module working in isolation but failing in integration specifically indicates an interaction problem rather than an internal logic error.

questions.question: Consider an AI-based image recognition system used for medical diagnosis. Why is applying traditional test oracles (expected output lists) particularly problematic for this system, and what alternative approach might testers use?
choices: Because the system is too complex; testers should skip testing entirely
Because medical images have infinite variations and expected outputs are difficult to define; testers might use metamorphic testing or confidence thresholds as oracle substitutes
Because the system is deterministic and produces the same output every time
Because AI systems never require testing for quality assurance
questions.explanation: Medical AI systems present a severe oracle problem since creating exhaustive lists of correct outputs for all possible images is infeasible. Metamorphic testing (verifying relationships between test cases) and statistical validation using confidence thresholds are pragmatic alternatives that address this challenge.

questions.question: A model-based testing approach using finite state machines (FSMs) is applied to an e-commerce checkout process. If the FSM has 5 states and 3 transitions per state, approximately how many system transitions must be covered for full transition pair coverage, and what quality insight does this provide?
choices: 15 transitions; provides insight into individual state functionality
25 transitions; ensures all single transitions are tested but misses interaction effects
45 transitions; verifies consecutive transition pairs to catch interaction defects between sequential states
125 transitions; guarantees absolute correctness of all possible execution paths
questions.explanation: Transition pair coverage requires testing consecutive transitions (n × n for n total transitions), which for 5 states with 3 transitions each yields approximately 45 test cases. This approach detects interaction defects between consecutive operations that single transition coverage might miss, providing better quality assurance than basic coverage metrics.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of mutation testing?
choices: To evaluate the effectiveness of a test suite by introducing intentional code changes
To automatically fix bugs in the source code
To replace traditional unit testing entirely
To identify memory leaks in applications
questions.explanation: Mutation testing measures test suite quality by introducing small mutations into code and checking if tests can detect these changes. A high mutation kill rate indicates a strong test suite.

questions.question: In mutation testing, what is an 'equivalent mutant'?
choices: A mutant that produces identical behavior to the original code despite being different
A mutant that is killed by exactly one test case
A mutant that introduces a new feature to the code
A mutant that increases code complexity
questions.explanation: Equivalent mutants are mutations that don't change the program's behavior semantically, making them impossible to kill with any test. They represent a limitation of mutation testing.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a property in property-based testing?
choices: A specific input-output pair that must be tested
A general assertion that should hold true for all inputs in a defined domain
A test case that runs exactly once
A performance metric for the system
questions.explanation: Properties in property-based testing are universal assertions that should be satisfied across a wide range of inputs. The testing framework generates diverse test cases to verify these properties hold.

questions.question: What is the mutation kill rate and how does it relate to test suite quality?
choices: The percentage of mutations that survive, indicating weak tests
The percentage of code lines covered by tests
The percentage of mutants killed by the test suite, where higher rates indicate stronger tests
The number of bugs found during mutation testing
questions.explanation: The kill rate is the proportion of introduced mutants that the test suite successfully detects and kills. A higher kill rate (closer to 100%) indicates a more effective test suite.

questions.question: Consider a function that calculates tax: `tax = salary * 0.15`. A mutation changes it to `tax = salary * 0.16`. Which type of test would most effectively kill this mutant?
choices: A test checking that the function accepts any positive number
A test with a known salary-tax pair that verifies the exact output value
A test that only checks if the function runs without crashing
A test measuring code execution time
questions.explanation: To kill a mutation affecting the calculation constant, tests need to verify exact output values. Testing with known input-output pairs (e.g., salary $100 should produce tax $15, not $16) will detect the mutant.

questions.question: How does property-based testing differ from traditional example-based testing, and what advantage does it provide for discovering bugs?
choices: Property-based testing uses fewer test cases but runs them multiple times sequentially
Property-based testing generates numerous varied test cases automatically and can discover unexpected edge cases that manual examples might miss
Property-based testing only works with mathematical functions
Property-based testing replaces the need for unit tests entirely
questions.explanation: Property-based testing automatically generates diverse inputs to find violations of stated properties, often uncovering edge cases that developers wouldn't think to test manually. This increases the likelihood of discovering subtle bugs.

questions.question: In designing mutation operators for a domain-specific language, why might a mutation operator that changes all instances of a logical AND (&&) to logical OR (||) be problematic, and what does this reveal about mutation testing limitations?
choices: It creates too many mutants and slows down testing
It may generate multiple equivalent mutants and inflated mutation scores if tests cannot distinguish between AND and OR in certain contexts
It violates the principles of test-driven development
It requires tests to be rewritten entirely
questions.explanation: A mutation operator that creates many equivalent mutants (e.g., AND to OR in cases where they behave identically) can artificially inflate kill rates, masking actual test suite weaknesses. This reveals that mutation testing effectiveness depends on carefully designed, semantically significant operators.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of mutation-based fuzzing compared to generation-based fuzzing?
choices: It requires fewer initial seed inputs and can discover bugs faster with less computational overhead
It generates completely random inputs without any knowledge of the target format
It requires detailed specifications of the input format before testing begins
It is more effective at finding security vulnerabilities in network protocols
questions.explanation: Mutation-based fuzzing leverages existing valid inputs as seeds and modifies them, requiring minimal setup compared to generation-based approaches which need formal specifications. This makes it more practical and faster in discovering bugs with less overhead.

questions.question: In AFL, what role does code coverage play in the fuzzing process?
choices: It measures how thoroughly the test suite exercises the source code
It guides the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that trigger new code paths and maximize exploration of the program
It determines the mutation rate applied to seed inputs
It is used only for reporting purposes and does not affect fuzzing decisions
questions.explanation: AFL uses coverage-guided fuzzing, where coverage feedback directs the fuzzer to preserve and mutate inputs that explore new code paths. This intelligent guidance dramatically improves bug discovery efficiency compared to random fuzzing.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how AFL's instrumentation mechanism works?
choices: It modifies the target program's binary to track runtime behavior and collect coverage information
It uses dynamic analysis without modifying the program code
It requires manual annotation of critical code sections by the developer
It works exclusively with open-source programs that provide source code access
questions.explanation: AFL instruments the target program during compilation (using afl-gcc or afl-clang) to embed coverage tracking code. This allows AFL to monitor which code paths are executed during fuzzing, enabling coverage-guided feedback.

questions.question: When using AFL, what is the significance of the 'hang' detection feature?
choices: It prevents the fuzzer from continuing after a certain time limit
It identifies infinite loops or excessive delays that may indicate performance bugs or denial-of-service vulnerabilities
It automatically terminates the fuzzing campaign
It records all inputs that take longer than average to process
questions.explanation: AFL's hang detection identifies inputs that cause the program to hang or execute indefinitely. These hangs often indicate infinite loops, deadlocks, or algorithmic issues that can be exploited as denial-of-service vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Explain how AFL's genetic algorithm approach to mutation differs from random mutation strategies in traditional fuzz testing.
choices: AFL applies all mutations simultaneously while traditional fuzzing applies one mutation at a time
AFL selectively breeds and mutates inputs that exhibit high code coverage, whereas random fuzzing treats all inputs equally regardless of their ability to explore new code
AFL uses only insertion mutations while traditional fuzzing uses deletion mutations
AFL requires a graphical user interface while traditional fuzzing operates only via command line
