questions.explanation: The bilinear transformation maps the entire s-axis to the unit circle in the z-plane, causing frequency warping where the relationship between continuous and discrete frequencies is nonlinear, especially near the Nyquist frequency. This distortion must be compensated through pre-warping techniques when designing controllers for mechatronic systems with stringent frequency response requirements.

questions.question: A discrete-time system has the transfer function G(z) = K(z + 0.5)/[(z - 0.8)(z - 0.9)]. For the system to be physically realizable and stable, and considering the system must have at least one sample of delay, which condition must be satisfied regarding the relationship between the number of poles and zeros?
choices: The number of zeros must equal the number of poles for physical realizability.
The number of poles must be greater than or equal to the number of zeros, with the difference representing the relative degree (delay); in this case satisfying the causality requirement.
The number of zeros must be greater than the number of poles by exactly one.
Poles and zeros must be conjugate pairs for the system to be physically realizable.
questions.explanation: For a discrete-time system to be causal (physically realizable), the number of poles must be greater than or equal to the number of zeros. The difference represents the relative degree, which corresponds to the number of sample delays. In this case, G(z) has 2 poles and 1 zero, so the relative degree is 1, indicating one sample delay. This ensures the system is realizable on digital hardware.

questions.question: For a discrete-time system to be stable, where must all poles be located in the z-plane?
choices: Inside the unit circle (|z| < 1)
Outside the unit circle (|z| > 1)
On the imaginary axis
On the real axis only
questions.explanation: A discrete-time system is stable if and only if all poles of its transfer function lie strictly inside the unit circle in the z-plane. Poles on or outside the unit circle indicate instability or marginal stability.

questions.question: A continuous-time system has a pole at s = -2. Using the zero-order hold discretization method with sampling period Ts = 0.1s, approximately where will this pole map to in the z-plane?
questions.explanation: Using zero-order hold discretization, a continuous pole at s maps to z = e^(sTs). For s = -2 and Ts = 0.1, z = e^(-0.2) ≈ 0.82. This pole remains inside the unit circle, preserving stability.

questions.question: Which discretization method provides exact matching of the system's response at sampling instants for systems with piecewise constant inputs?
choices: Bilinear (Tustin) transformation
Zero-order hold equivalence method
Backward difference method
Pole-zero mapping
questions.explanation: The zero-order hold (ZOH) equivalence method assumes the input is held constant between samples and produces a discretized system that exactly matches the continuous-time system's response at the sampling instants. This is ideal for systems with piecewise constant inputs.

questions.question: A continuous-time system has the state-space representation: ẋ = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du. When discretizing using the zero-order hold method with sampling period Ts, which of the following represents the discretized state transition matrix Ad?
choices: Ad = A × Ts
Ad = e^(A·Ts)
Ad = I + A + A²/(2!)Ts²
questions.explanation: The discretized state transition matrix for zero-order hold discretization is given by Ad = e^(A·Ts), which represents the matrix exponential. This preserves the system dynamics over the sampling interval.

questions.question: A discrete-time transfer function has a pole at z = 0.5 and another at z = 1.05. What can be concluded about the system's stability?
choices: The system is stable because the average magnitude is less than 1
The system is unstable because one pole is outside the unit circle
The system is marginally stable and will oscillate
Stability cannot be determined without knowing the zeros
questions.explanation: The system is unstable because at least one pole (z = 1.05) lies outside the unit circle. For stability, ALL poles must be strictly inside the unit circle. The pole at z = 0.5 alone is not sufficient to ensure stability.

questions.question: When using the bilinear (Tustin) transformation for discretization, the continuous-time s-plane maps to the z-plane according to which relationship?
choices: z = e^(sTs)
z = s × Ts
questions.explanation: The bilinear transformation uses the approximation s ≈ (2/Ts) × (z-1)/(z+1), which can be rearranged to show z = (1 + sTs/2)/(1 - sTs/2). This method provides good frequency response matching and always maps the left half s-plane to the interior of the unit circle in the z-plane.

questions.question: A continuous-time system with transfer function Gc(s) = 1/(s+1) is discretized using zero-order hold with Ts = 0.1s. The discretized input matrix Bd = ∫₀^Ts e^(A·τ) dτ × B must account for what aspect of the continuous system?
choices: The steady-state gain of the system only
The rate at which the system responds to input changes during the sampling interval
The number of zeros in the transfer function
The phase margin of the original continuous system
questions.explanation: The discretized input matrix Bd = ∫₀^Ts e^(A·τ) dτ × B captures how the system accumulates and responds to inputs over the entire sampling interval Ts. It accounts for the integral effect of the continuous dynamics between sample times, which is crucial for accurate discretization.

questions.question: In discrete controller design, what is the primary purpose of pole-zero cancellation?
choices: To eliminate undesirable poles and simplify the closed-loop system dynamics
To increase the system bandwidth indefinitely
To guarantee zero steady-state error for all input types
To reduce the sampling period of the system
questions.explanation: Pole-zero cancellation removes problematic poles from the closed-loop transfer function, simplifying the system response and improving control performance. While it can improve steady-state error, that is not its primary purpose, and it does not affect sampling period.

questions.question: When designing a discrete controller using root locus, which of the following statements about the z-plane is correct?
choices: All poles must lie outside the unit circle for stability
All poles must lie inside the unit circle for stability
Pole location is independent of sampling time
Complex poles must always appear in conjugate pairs on the real axis
questions.explanation: For discrete-time systems, stability requires all closed-loop poles to be located inside the unit circle in the z-plane. Poles outside the unit circle represent unstable modes that grow without bound.

questions.question: A discrete system has an undesired pole at z = 0.5. To cancel this pole using pole-zero cancellation, where should the controller zero be placed?
choices: At z = -0.5 to create a stable combination
At z = 0.5 to directly cancel the pole
At z = 2.0 to move the pole further inside the unit circle
At z = 0.25 to reduce the pole's magnitude
questions.explanation: Pole-zero cancellation requires placing a controller zero at the same location as the pole to be cancelled. In this case, placing a zero at z = 0.5 will cancel the pole at z = 0.5, removing it from the closed-loop dynamics.

questions.question: In root locus analysis for discrete controller design, what does the angle criterion determine?
choices: The magnitude of the controller gain required
The locus of points where the phase contribution from poles and zeros equals 180°
The maximum allowable sampling frequency
The steady-state error of the system
questions.explanation: The angle criterion in root locus states that a point in the z-plane lies on the root locus if the sum of angles from zeros minus the sum of angles from poles equals 180° (or odd multiples thereof). This forms the basis for constructing the root locus curve.

questions.question: A discrete controller is designed to place closed-loop poles at z = 0.6 ± j0.3. What can be inferred about the system's transient response?
choices: The system is unstable because the poles are complex
The system is stable with oscillatory response due to the complex conjugate poles and damping determined by their magnitude
The system has zero overshoot regardless of the reference input
The response time cannot be determined from pole location alone
questions.explanation: Complex conjugate poles inside the unit circle indicate a stable, oscillatory response. The magnitude √(0.6² + 0.3²) ≈ 0.67 indicates moderate damping, and the phase angle relates to oscillation frequency. Poles on the unit circle would cause marginal stability.

questions.question: Consider designing a discrete controller with a lead compensator (zero at z = 0.4, pole at z = 0.2) for a system with an open-loop pole at z = 0.9. Using root locus principles, explain how this compensator affects the closed-loop pole locations compared to uncompensated design. Which statement best describes the effect?
choices: The lead compensator has no effect on pole location since its gain does not enter the root locus
The lead compensator pulls the root locus toward the left (toward the zero at z = 0.4), allowing placement of closed-loop poles at more desirable locations with finite gain
The lead compensator always makes the system unstable by moving poles outside the unit circle
The effect depends entirely on the sampling period and cannot be predicted without numerical simulation
questions.explanation: Lead compensators modify the root locus by introducing a zero that attracts the root locus branches toward it, enabling placement of closed-loop poles at better locations (smaller magnitude, less oscillatory). The pole of the compensator at z = 0.2 slightly modifies the locus shape. This is a fundamental application of root locus design.

questions.question: A discrete system requires a closed-loop pole at z = 0.5 to achieve desired settling time. The open-loop pole is at z = 0.8 and there are no open-loop zeros. Using the magnitude criterion, what must be the controller gain K to place a closed-loop pole at z = 0.5?
choices: K = 0.6 because the gain must equal the pole location
K = 0.3 from the magnitude criterion: |K/(0.5-0.8)| = 1, yielding K = 0.3
K cannot be determined without knowing the sampling time and system order
questions.explanation: The magnitude criterion states that at any point on the root locus, |K · (zeros product)/(poles product)| = 1. For a desired closed-loop pole at z = 0.5 with only an open-loop pole at z = 0.8 and no zeros: K/|0.5 - 0.8| = 1, so K = 0.3. This value ensures the pole placement satisfies both angle and magnitude criteria.

questions.question: In Ragazzini's direct design method, what is the primary advantage of working in the z-domain rather than the s-domain for discrete controller design?
choices: It directly relates to the actual discrete-time behavior of the system without requiring bilinear transformation approximations
It simplifies the calculation of continuous-time system parameters
It eliminates the need for sampling time considerations
It guarantees stability for all pole locations within the unit circle
questions.explanation: The z-domain directly represents the discrete-time behavior of sampled systems, avoiding approximation errors that arise from continuous-to-discrete transformations. The z-domain is the natural domain for discrete-time analysis where stability requires poles inside the unit circle.

questions.question: When designing a discrete controller using Ragazzini's method, what does specifying the desired closed-loop transfer function Hd(z) accomplish?
choices: It directly provides the controller parameters without further calculation
It establishes the performance specifications that the closed-loop system must satisfy, including settling time and steady-state error
It guarantees the controller will be physically realizable
It determines the sampling frequency required for implementation
questions.explanation: Hd(z) is chosen to reflect desired transient response characteristics (settling time, overshoot) and steady-state performance. Once specified, the actual controller D(z) is derived from the relationship between the desired closed-loop response and the plant dynamics, making it a crucial design specification step.

questions.question: In Ragazzini's method, if you specify pole locations at z = 0.5 and z = 0.3 for a second-order system, what can you conclude about the system response?
choices: The system will have a long settling time with high overshoot due to poles near the imaginary axis
The system will settle quickly with minimal overshoot since both poles are real and well inside the unit circle
The system will oscillate indefinitely because poles are not at the origin
The system stability cannot be determined without knowing the sampling period
questions.explanation: Poles at z = 0.5 and z = 0.3 are real, distinct, and located well inside the unit circle, indicating fast convergence without oscillation. Real poles in the z-domain correspond to non-oscillatory responses, and their proximity to the origin determines the speed of decay.

questions.question: Which of the following constraints must be satisfied when deriving D(z) from the desired closed-loop transfer function Hd(z) and plant model Gp(z)?
choices: The controller transfer function must have more zeros than poles to ensure physical realizability
The order of D(z) must equal the order of Gp(z) for stability
D(z) must be causal, meaning it cannot depend on future values of the input or output
All poles of D(z) must lie exactly on the unit circle for stability
questions.explanation: Causality is a fundamental constraint in practical controller implementation—the controller output at time k can only depend on current and past values, not future values. This restricts the form of D(z) and must be verified when deriving the controller from design specifications.

questions.question: A discrete controller designed using Ragazzini's method yields D(z) = (z² + 2z + 1)/(z³ - 0.5z² + 0.1z). What issue might arise when attempting to implement this controller?
choices: The controller is non-causal because the numerator degree exceeds the denominator degree, violating physical realizability
The controller is unstable because not all poles lie on the unit circle
The controller cannot be discretized from a continuous-time equivalent
The controller will produce unbounded outputs due to the repeated factor in the numerator
questions.explanation: For a discrete controller to be causal and realizable, the degree of the denominator must be greater than or equal to the degree of the numerator. Here, the numerator has degree 2 while the denominator has degree 3, which is acceptable. Actually, this controller is causal. The question tests understanding that non-causality occurs when the numerator degree exceeds denominator degree.

questions.question: In Ragazzini's method, you must choose the desired closed-loop poles to achieve a settling time of 0.5 seconds with a sampling period of 0.1 seconds. Approximately how many sampling periods should the dominant pole decay envelope span to meet this specification?
choices: Approximately 10 to 20 sampling periods; the dominant pole should be around z ≈ 0.1 to 0.3
Approximately 5 to 7 sampling periods; the dominant pole should be around z ≈ 0.1 to 0.2
Approximately 2 to 3 sampling periods; the dominant pole should be around z ≈ 0.6 to 0.8
The sampling period and settling time specification are independent considerations in discrete design
questions.explanation: Settling time of 0.5 seconds with 0.1-second sampling period means approximately 5 sampling periods. The pole should satisfy z = e^(-nTs/τ) where the decay time constant τ relates to settling time. For 5 periods of decay to 2% settling, the pole magnitude should be approximately 0.1-0.2, requiring roughly 5-7 sampling intervals for adequate settling.

questions.question: When applying Ragazzini's direct design method, which statement best describes the relationship between the desired closed-loop transfer function Hd(z), the plant Gp(z), and the controller D(z)?
choices: Hd(z) = D(z) · Gp(z) / (1 + D(z) · Gp(z)), which is rearranged to solve for D(z)
D(z) is chosen independently of Hd(z) and Gp(z) based solely on pole placement rules
Hd(z) and D(z) are identical in form; the controller simply implements the desired response directly
The controller D(z) must be designed first, then Hd(z) is calculated to verify performance
questions.explanation: Ragazzini's method starts with the closed-loop equation Hd(z) = D(z)·Gp(z)/(1 + D(z)·Gp(z)). The designer specifies Hd(z) based on performance requirements, then solves for D(z) = Hd(z) / [Gp(z)(1 - Hd(z))]. This algebraic relationship is fundamental to the direct analytical design approach.

questions.question: When designing a controller using the Bode method for indirect discrete design, what is the primary advantage of working in the continuous-time domain first?
choices: Continuous-time design tools and frequency response methods are more mature and intuitive than discrete-time equivalents
Discretization is unnecessary if the sampling frequency is high enough
Discrete-time Bode plots cannot be plotted accurately
Continuous-time controllers are always more stable than discrete controllers
questions.explanation: Continuous-time frequency response design methods are well-established and provide intuitive tools for shaping gain and phase margins. Once the continuous controller is designed, it can be discretized using standard methods. Discretization is necessary regardless of sampling frequency to implement the controller digitally.

questions.question: In the indirect design method, after designing a compensator G_c(s) using Bode analysis, which discretization method preserves the frequency response most accurately at lower frequencies?
choices: Forward Euler substitution
Tustin's method (bilinear transformation)
Backward Euler substitution
Zero-order hold approximation alone
questions.explanation: Tustin's method provides better frequency response matching compared to Euler methods because it maps the jω axis more accurately, preserving characteristics at lower frequencies. This makes it superior for maintaining the controller's performance when transitioning from continuous to discrete time.

questions.question: A continuous-time controller is designed with a gain margin of 12 dB and phase margin of 45° at the crossover frequency. After discretization using Tustin's method with a sampling period T_s = 0.01 s, which statement is most likely true?
choices: The gain and phase margins will increase slightly due to the discretization process
The gain and phase margins will remain virtually unchanged because Tustin's method is frequency-preserving at lower frequencies
The gain and phase margins will decrease significantly, requiring redesign
The phase margin will increase while the gain margin decreases
questions.explanation: Tustin's method provides a conformal mapping that preserves frequency response characteristics particularly well at frequencies much lower than the Nyquist frequency. With adequate sampling (ω_s >> 2ω_c), the margins should remain very close to the continuous-time design values.

questions.question: When applying the indirect design method to a mechatronic system with a crossover frequency of 50 rad/s, what is the minimum recommended sampling frequency to ensure the discretized controller maintains adequate performance?
choices: 50 rad/s (equal to crossover frequency)
100 rad/s (2× crossover frequency)
500 rad/s (10× crossover frequency)
1000 rad/s (20× crossover frequency)
questions.explanation: For indirect design using continuous-frequency response methods, a minimum sampling rate of 10-20 times the crossover frequency is recommended to ensure that the discretized controller maintains the designed frequency response characteristics and avoids significant warping effects at the control bandwidth.

questions.question: You designed a proportional-integral (PI) controller G_c(s) = K_p + K_i/s using Bode methods to achieve a phase margin of 50° at ω_c = 30 rad/s. After discretizing using Tustin's method with T_s = 0.05 s, you notice the actual phase margin in simulation is only 35°. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Tustin's method is inherently unsuitable for PI controllers
The sampling period is too large relative to the bandwidth, causing frequency warping and phase lag at the crossover frequency
The gain K_p was calculated incorrectly in the original design
PI controllers cannot be discretized using Tustin's method
questions.explanation: With T_s = 0.05 s and ω_c = 30 rad/s, the Nyquist frequency is only 125.6 rad/s, making the sampling rate approximately 4.2× the crossover frequency. This violates the recommended 10-20× rule, causing significant frequency warping in the Tustin transformation, which reduces the phase margin at the designed crossover frequency.

questions.question: In an indirect design workflow, after discretizing a continuous compensator, you perform closed-loop simulation and find that the discrete system becomes unstable while the continuous-time analysis predicted stability. Which combination of factors is most likely responsible?
choices: The continuous-time design had insufficient phase margin and the discretization was performed correctly
Unmodeled delays in the discrete implementation exceed 1/10 of the sampling period, and the sampling frequency is inadequate relative to the control bandwidth
Tustin's method was applied with a gain adjustment factor
The discrete-time system has a different pole-zero structure by design
questions.explanation: Instability arising after correct discretization typically results from unmodeled delays (computational, sensor, actuator) combined with insufficient sampling rates. When the sampling rate is not fast enough relative to bandwidth, discretization errors accumulate, and delays become more destabilizing. This necessitates either increasing sampling rate or reducing controller bandwidth.

questions.question: A mechatronic system requires a discrete controller with crossover frequency 40 rad/s and 55° phase margin. You plan to use the indirect design method with Tustin's discretization. If you select T_s = 0.001 s, what is the primary trade-off you face compared to selecting T_s = 0.01 s?
choices: Smaller T_s guarantees a larger phase margin regardless of controller design
Smaller T_s increases computational burden and cost while providing better frequency response matching and reduced discretization error
Smaller T_s eliminates the need for frequency response analysis
Smaller T_s makes the controller more sensitive to measurement noise
questions.explanation: Smaller sampling periods provide better frequency response matching and reduce discretization error, allowing the designed controller performance to transfer more accurately to the discrete implementation. However, this comes at the cost of increased computational requirements and potentially higher hardware costs, requiring careful cost-benefit analysis for real-time implementation.

questions.question: For a state feedback control law u = -Kx, what is the primary advantage of using pole placement over arbitrary gain selection?
choices: It guarantees that all closed-loop poles are placed at desired locations to achieve specified performance requirements
It reduces computational burden by eliminating the need for matrix inversion
It automatically ensures the system is stable regardless of initial conditions
It minimizes energy consumption of the actuators
questions.explanation: Pole placement allows designers to directly specify closed-loop eigenvalues, ensuring desired transient response characteristics and stability margins. This is the fundamental purpose of pole placement design methodology in state feedback control.

questions.question: A system has the characteristic that its state variables cannot be completely determined from measurements of its output. Which fundamental property is violated?
choices: Controllability
Observability
Stability
Reachability
questions.explanation: Observability is the property that ensures all state variables can be uniquely determined from input and output measurements over a finite time interval. If states cannot be reconstructed from outputs, the system lacks observability, which is essential for observer design.

questions.question: In Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) design, increasing the weight on control effort in the cost function J = ∫(x'Qx + u'Ru)dt will have which effect on the feedback gain K?
choices: The gain K will increase, resulting in more aggressive control
The gain K will decrease, producing more conservative control with less energy usage
The gain K will remain unchanged as it is independent of R
The gain K will oscillate between positive and negative values
questions.explanation: Increasing R penalizes control input more heavily in the LQR optimization, forcing the algorithm to find gains that use less control energy. This results in smaller magnitude feedback gains and more conservative control action to minimize overall cost.

questions.question: For a state observer with estimation error dynamics ė = (A - LC)e, what condition must be satisfied to ensure that estimation errors decay to zero?
choices: The eigenvalues of (A - LC) must have positive real parts
The eigenvalues of (A - LC) must have negative real parts and the system must be controllable
The eigenvalues of (A - LC) must have negative real parts and the system must be observable
The matrix L must equal the identity matrix
questions.explanation: Observer error convergence requires that all eigenvalues of (A - LC) lie in the left half of the complex plane (negative real parts). Observability is a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a gain L that achieves arbitrary pole placement for the error dynamics.

questions.question: The separation principle in control theory states that:
choices: State feedback and observer design can be performed independently, and the combined system stability is guaranteed if both subsystems are individually stable
The controller and observer must be designed simultaneously to avoid instability
Observability and controllability are mutually exclusive properties
Full state feedback always provides better performance than output feedback
questions.explanation: The separation principle allows independent design of the state feedback controller and state observer. If both the closed-loop system (with full state feedback) and the observer error dynamics are asymptotically stable, then the combined controller-observer system is also stable.

questions.question: Consider a 3rd-order system where you want to design a state observer with eigenvalues at -5, -6, and -8. Which condition must you verify first before proceeding with observer gain calculation?
choices: Verify that the system is controllable by checking the rank of the controllability matrix
Verify that the system is observable by checking the rank of the observability matrix [C; CA; CA²]
Verify that all desired eigenvalues satisfy the Hurwitz criterion
Verify that the system has no repeated eigenvalues
questions.explanation: Observability must be verified before designing a state observer because it is a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of observer gains that can place the error dynamics at arbitrary locations. The observability matrix must have full rank (rank = n) for the system to be observable.

questions.question: In a combined state feedback controller-observer system where the controller uses estimated states x̂ instead of true states x, the closed-loop error dynamics include both control error (x) and estimation error (ẽ = x - x̂). How are these errors coupled?
choices: The errors are fully coupled; the control error dynamics depend on the estimation error, and vice versa
The control error dynamics depend on estimation error, but estimation error dynamics are decoupled from control error due to the separation principle
The errors are completely decoupled and can be analyzed independently
The coupling depends on whether the system is linear or nonlinear
questions.explanation: The separation principle ensures that estimation error dynamics (ė = (A - LC)ẽ) are independent of control performance, while control error dynamics depend on the total error. This decoupling is fundamental and allows independent design of both subsystems while maintaining overall system stability.

questions.question: A continuous-time LTI system is described by the state equation ẋ = Ax + Bu. What is the primary advantage of converting this system to discrete-time form using the Euler approximation method?
choices: It allows implementation on digital computers and controllers with finite sampling rates
It eliminates the need for state observers in the system
It guarantees stability regardless of the sampling period chosen
It reduces the number of state variables required
questions.explanation: Discrete-time approximation enables real-time implementation on digital systems with specific sampling periods, which is essential for autonomous systems. The Euler method provides a simple computational approach, though stability depends on proper sampling period selection.

questions.question: For a MIMO system with 3 inputs and 4 outputs, what are the dimensions of the input matrix B if the system has 5 state variables?
questions.explanation: In the state equation ẋ = Ax + Bu, matrix B must be (n × m) where n is the number of states (5) and m is the number of inputs (3). Therefore, B is 5 × 3 to properly multiply with the input vector u.

questions.question: A nonlinear system's behavior depends heavily on the operating point. Which of the following statements best describes how this affects state-space analysis?
choices: Nonlinear systems cannot be analyzed using state-space methods under any circumstances
Nonlinear systems can be linearized around equilibrium points to yield approximately valid LTI models in small regions, but lose validity far from equilibrium
Nonlinear systems automatically become LTV systems when expressed in state-space form
The nonlinearity is eliminated when state variables are properly chosen
questions.explanation: Linearization around equilibrium points is a standard technique for analyzing nonlinear systems locally. The Taylor series expansion creates an LTI approximation valid near the operating point, but accuracy degrades for large deviations.

questions.question: A state observer is designed to estimate unmeasurable state variables. If the observer gain matrix L is chosen with eigenvalues that are too far left in the complex plane, what undesirable consequence might occur?
choices: The observed states will converge too slowly to actual values
The observer will require excessive computational power and may amplify measurement noise
The observer will become unstable and diverge from actual states
The system will automatically switch to open-loop control
questions.explanation: While faster convergence (further left eigenvalues) improves tracking, it requires larger observer gains that amplify measurement noise and increase sensitivity to disturbances, potentially causing practical implementation issues in real autonomous systems.

questions.question: Consider a robot operating in both a body-fixed frame and an inertial frame. A velocity vector is measured as [2, 1] m/s in the body frame. If the robot is rotated 90° counterclockwise relative to the inertial frame, what is the velocity vector in the inertial frame?
questions.explanation: A 90° counterclockwise rotation matrix is [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. Multiplying this by [2, 1]ᵀ gives [0·2 + (-1)·1, 1·2 + 0·1]ᵀ = [-1, 2]ᵀ. Coordinate transformations are critical in autonomous systems for proper sensor fusion and control.

questions.question: In implementing a discrete-time approximation using the bilinear transformation (Tustin method) instead of forward Euler, what is a significant advantage when controlling high-bandwidth autonomous systems?
choices: It requires fewer computational steps than Euler approximation
It better preserves system stability margins and handles higher frequencies more accurately before aliasing occurs
It eliminates the need for state observers entirely
It automatically compensates for all nonlinearities in the system
questions.explanation: The bilinear transformation maps the entire s-plane's left-half to the unit circle in the z-plane, providing better frequency response matching and stability preservation compared to Euler methods. This is particularly important for autonomous systems with multiple control loops operating at different frequencies.

questions.question: A MIMO system with state-space realization (A, B, C, D) is transformed by a change of coordinates: z = Tx where T is invertible. Derive which of the following matrices changes under this transformation, and how does it affect observability?
choices: Only the B and D matrices change; observability is unaffected because the eigenvalues of (C·A^n) remain constant
The A matrix remains unchanged; the C matrix becomes CT⁻¹, and observability is preserved because rank(O) = rank(O_new) for the observability matrix
All matrices change including D; observability may be lost if T is poorly conditioned
The D matrix alone determines observability, which is independent of coordinate transformations
questions.explanation: Under coordinate transformation z = Tx, the new realization becomes (T⁻¹AT, T⁻¹B, CT⁻¹, D). The observability matrix O = [C; CA; ...] transforms such that its rank is preserved, meaning unobservable modes remain unobservable. This is fundamental for proving observability is a structural property independent of coordinates.

questions.question: In dead reckoning, what is the primary source of error accumulation over time?
choices: Integration of sensor noise and measurement drift leading to unbounded position error
Loss of GPS signal in indoor environments
Excessive computational load on the processor
Insufficient battery power for sensor operation
questions.explanation: Dead reckoning relies on integrating velocity and orientation estimates, and any small errors in these measurements accumulate over time, causing position estimates to drift significantly. This is why periodic external references (like landmarks) are necessary for correction.

questions.question: Which kinematic model assumption is most critical for accurate dead reckoning in ground robots?
choices: The robot can instantaneously change velocity in any direction
No-slip condition: the robot moves in the direction it is oriented without sideways slipping
The robot's mass is negligible and dynamics can be ignored
All wheels have identical radii and operate synchronously
questions.explanation: The no-slip assumption is fundamental to kinematic models for wheeled robots, ensuring that velocity and orientation estimates directly correspond to actual position changes. Violations of this assumption (e.g., on slippery surfaces) lead to significant dead reckoning errors.

questions.question: A 2D LiDAR sensor provides range measurements at multiple angles. What is a key limitation when using LiDAR alone for autonomous navigation?
choices: It cannot measure the height of obstacles, only their presence in the horizontal plane
It requires constant calibration every hour of operation
It cannot detect moving objects in real-time
It consumes more power than RGB cameras
questions.explanation: 2D LiDAR scans a horizontal plane and measures distances in that plane only, making it unable to detect obstacles above or below the scanning plane. This is why 3D sensors or multiple 2D LiDAR units at different heights are needed for full spatial awareness.

questions.question: How does a 3D IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) differ from a 2D LiDAR in terms of information provided?
choices: An IMU measures relative motion and orientation changes through accelerometers and gyroscopes, while LiDAR measures absolute distances to environmental features
An IMU is more accurate for obstacle detection than LiDAR
An IMU can directly measure position without integration
An IMU detects colors while LiDAR detects only depth
questions.explanation: IMUs are proprioceptive sensors that measure the robot's own motion through acceleration and rotation rates, requiring integration for position estimates. LiDAR is exteroceptive, measuring the environment directly. They complement each other: LiDAR corrects IMU drift, while IMU provides high-frequency motion data.

questions.question: In an RGB-D camera system, what advantage does the depth information provide over a standard RGB camera for autonomous systems?
choices: It enables 3D scene reconstruction and obstacle avoidance without requiring stereo matching algorithms or external depth estimation
It improves color accuracy in low-light conditions
It reduces the amount of data that needs to be transmitted
It eliminates the need for any other sensors in the robot
questions.explanation: RGB-D cameras directly capture depth data using structured light or time-of-flight technology, providing 3D information immediately. This is more efficient than standard RGB cameras, which require stereo correspondence or other complex algorithms to estimate depth, making RGB-D superior for real-time obstacle detection and mapping.

questions.question: Consider a robot performing dead reckoning in an indoor environment using wheel encoders and an IMU. After 10 minutes of continuous motion, the estimated position has drifted significantly from the actual position. Which sensor fusion approach would most effectively correct this drift while maintaining the benefits of dead reckoning?
choices: Replace the IMU with a more expensive gyroscope that has lower noise
Integrate LiDAR or visual landmarks to provide periodic absolute position corrections while using dead reckoning between corrections
Increase the frequency of encoder readings to reduce quantization error
Use only the IMU and ignore encoder data to reduce computational complexity
questions.explanation: This is a classic application of sensor fusion and localization. Dead reckoning provides continuous, high-frequency motion estimates but drifts over time. External sensors like LiDAR or visual landmarks can detect known features in the environment to provide absolute position corrections, which reset the accumulated drift while maintaining the advantages of dead reckoning between corrections.

questions.question: A Project 1 implementation requires a robot to navigate through a cluttered indoor environment using an RGB-D camera and an IMU. The robot must avoid obstacles and maintain accurate position estimates. What is the most critical consideration when integrating these two sensors, and why might RGB-D alone be insufficient?
choices: RGB-D cameras have limited range (typically 3-5 meters) and can be affected by lighting conditions, so the IMU's inertial measurements help predict motion when visual features are absent or unreliable, enabling robust navigation through vision-denied areas
The RGB-D camera is always more accurate than the IMU, so the IMU should only be used as a backup
RGB-D and IMU operate at different frequencies, so they cannot be used together
The RGB-D camera can measure distance accurately but cannot provide angular velocity information, which the IMU provides
questions.explanation: While RGB-D is excellent for obstacle detection and feature-based localization, it has inherent limitations: finite range, susceptibility to lighting conditions, and potential loss of features in featureless areas. The IMU provides continuous motion measurements independent of the environment, enabling the robot to maintain position estimates during visual outages. A robust system fuses both: RGB-D for absolute corrections and obstacle detection, IMU for continuous motion prediction.

questions.question: In map-based localization, what is the primary role of the cost function in an optimization framework?
choices: To quantify the difference between predicted sensor measurements and actual observations
To store the map data in memory efficiently
To define the robot's movement constraints
To calibrate the camera intrinsic parameters
questions.explanation: The cost function measures how well a candidate pose explains the observed sensor data relative to the map. Minimizing this function finds the pose that best matches the measurements, which is fundamental to optimization-based localization.

questions.question: Which optimization technique is most commonly used for real-time map-based localization in autonomous systems?
choices: Genetic algorithms with population size of 1000
Gradient descent or Gauss-Newton methods on the pose parameters
Exhaustive grid search over the entire map
Simulated annealing with multiple temperature schedules
questions.explanation: Gradient descent and Gauss-Newton methods are computationally efficient and converge quickly, making them suitable for real-time localization. They directly optimize pose parameters by iteratively reducing the localization error based on sensor-map mismatches.

questions.question: A robot uses LiDAR to scan its environment and matches point cloud data against a pre-built occupancy grid map. What does the optimization process minimize in this scenario?
choices: The distance between the robot and the nearest obstacle
The sum of squared differences between expected and observed LiDAR readings at the candidate pose
The entropy of the occupancy grid
The total cost of map storage
questions.explanation: The optimization minimizes the residual error between what the LiDAR should observe at each candidate pose versus what it actually observes. This least-squares approach finds the pose that produces the best agreement between predicted and measured sensor data.

questions.question: Why is the Jacobian matrix critical when applying Newton-based optimization methods to pose estimation in map-based localization?
choices: It represents the gradient of the cost function with respect to pose parameters, enabling efficient iterative refinement
It stores the raw sensor measurements from the LiDAR
It defines the boundaries of the valid localization region
It compresses the map data for faster transmission
questions.explanation: The Jacobian provides first-order derivative information about how the cost function changes with small pose perturbations. This enables Newton methods to compute descent directions and step sizes efficiently, leading to fast convergence to the optimal pose.

questions.question: Consider a map-based localization system where the optimization converges to a local minimum instead of the global minimum. What is the most practical consequence for autonomous system navigation?
choices: The robot will perfectly localize but move very slowly
The robot estimates an incorrect pose that still satisfies some sensor-map constraints, leading to potential navigation errors and drift over time
The map data will become corrupted
The LiDAR will stop functioning
questions.explanation: Convergence to a local minimum means the optimization finds a suboptimal pose that may partially match the map but is not the true location. This can cause the robot to navigate based on incorrect position estimates, accumulating errors and eventually failing localization.

questions.question: An autonomous vehicle uses bundle adjustment to jointly optimize its trajectory poses and landmark positions while localizing against a map. How does this nonlinear optimization approach differ from estimating pose independently at each timestep?
choices: Bundle adjustment is faster because it ignores temporal information
Bundle adjustment solves a larger coupled optimization problem that uses inter-pose constraints and landmark consistency to improve accuracy and reduce drift
Bundle adjustment is only applicable to monocular cameras, not multi-sensor systems
Bundle adjustment requires no iteration and provides solutions in closed form
questions.explanation: Bundle adjustment formulates localization as a large nonlinear optimization that couples multiple poses and observations, enforcing consistency across the entire trajectory. This global approach reduces accumulated errors and provides more robust estimates than independent per-frame optimization, though it requires iterative nonlinear solvers.

questions.question: In a map-based localization system using Levenberg-Marquardt optimization, when would a practitioner increase the damping parameter λ, and what does this adjustment accomplish?
choices: Increase λ when convergence is fast to make the algorithm run even faster; it shifts the algorithm toward steepest descent for stability near poor local minima
Increase λ when the algorithm diverges or oscillates; it shifts the algorithm toward steepest descent for more conservative steps and improved stability when far from the optimum
Increase λ to reduce memory consumption of the Jacobian matrix
Decrease λ values, as increasing λ always causes divergence in localization problems
questions.explanation: Levenberg-Marquardt interpolates between Gauss-Newton (fast near optimum) and steepest descent (stable far away). Increasing λ biases toward steepest descent with smaller steps, which helps stabilize optimization when the current pose estimate is poor or the algorithm begins oscillating.

questions.question: A random variable X has probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. What is P(X > 0.5)?
questions.explanation: Integrating the PDF from 0.5 to 1: ∫₀.₅¹ 2x dx = [x²]₀.₅¹ = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75. This demonstrates understanding of how to compute probabilities from a given PDF.

questions.question: For two random variables X and Y with joint PDF f(x,y), the marginal PDF of X is obtained by:
choices: Differentiating f(x,y) with respect to x
Integrating f(x,y) over all possible values of y
Setting y to zero in f(x,y)
Multiplying f(x,y) by the PDF of Y
questions.explanation: The marginal PDF is defined as f_X(x) = ∫₋∞^∞ f(x,y) dy, eliminating the dependence on Y through integration. This is fundamental to reducing joint distributions to individual variable distributions.

questions.question: Two independent random variables X and Y have joint PDF f(x,y). Which statement is correct?
choices: f(x,y) = f_X(x) + f_Y(y)
f(x,y) = f_X(x) · f_Y(y)
f(x|y) depends on the value of y
The conditional PDF f(x|y) equals f_Y(y)
questions.explanation: For independent random variables, the joint PDF factors into the product of marginal PDFs: f(x,y) = f_X(x) · f_Y(y). Additionally, for independent variables, f(x|y) = f_X(x), showing that knowing Y provides no information about X.

questions.question: White noise in a discrete-time signal has which of the following properties?
choices: Highly correlated samples with zero mean
Uncorrelated samples with zero mean and constant variance
Deterministic periodic oscillations
Correlation function that varies linearly with time lag
questions.explanation: White noise is characterized by samples that are statistically independent (uncorrelated), have zero mean, and constant variance across all time lags. This makes it ideal for modeling sensor noise in autonomous systems.

questions.question: In Bayesian estimation, what does Bayes' Rule express?
choices: The relationship between prior and likelihood probabilities only
The posterior probability as proportional to the likelihood times the prior
That the prior probability equals the posterior probability
The conditional independence of all random variables
questions.explanation: Bayes' Rule states P(θ|data) ∝ P(data|θ)·P(θ), where the posterior is proportional to the likelihood multiplied by the prior. This fundamental equation enables updating beliefs about parameters θ based on observed data.

questions.question: A sensor measures position X with Gaussian noise, giving measurement Z = X + N where N ~ N(0, σ²). If the prior on X is uniform over [0, 10], what can be inferred about the posterior distribution of X after observing Z?
choices: The posterior is always uniform, regardless of the measurement
The posterior will be a Gaussian distribution centered closer to Z than the prior mean
The posterior depends only on the prior and is independent of the likelihood
The posterior cannot be computed without knowing the exact measurement value Z
questions.explanation: Using Bayes' Rule, the posterior is proportional to the Gaussian likelihood (centered at Z) times the uniform prior. This results in a Gaussian posterior distribution shifted toward the measurement Z, demonstrating how measurements update prior beliefs in autonomous system state estimation.

questions.question: For a multivariate system with state vector X = [X₁, X₂]ᵀ and correlated components, explain why examining only the marginal PDFs f(x₁) and f(x₂) separately could lead to incorrect system behavior predictions.
choices: Marginal PDFs contain redundant information that causes computational errors
Marginal PDFs discard information about statistical dependence between X₁ and X₂, preventing accurate prediction of joint outcomes
Marginal PDFs are always undefined for correlated random variables
The joint PDF is always equal to the sum of marginal PDFs for any system
questions.explanation: Marginal PDFs only describe individual variable distributions and lose all information about their dependence structure. For example, knowing f(x₁) and f(x₂) separately cannot capture correlation: two variables could be positively or negatively correlated, or independent, yet have identical marginals. In autonomous systems, ignoring these dependencies leads to poor state estimation and control performance.

questions.question: Which property of Gaussian random variables makes the Kalman Filter optimal for linear systems with Gaussian noise?
choices: Gaussians are closed under linear transformations, preserving optimality of linear estimators
Gaussians have the smallest variance among all distributions
Gaussians require less computational power than other distributions
Gaussians are the only distributions that can represent uncertainty
questions.explanation: The Kalman Filter achieves optimality because linear transformations of Gaussian variables remain Gaussian, and the linear minimum mean square error (LMMSE) estimator is optimal for Gaussian distributions. This mathematical property ensures the filter produces the best possible state estimate.

questions.question: In a Kalman Filter update step, what does the Kalman gain matrix K determine?
choices: The rate at which the system state changes over time
How much the measurement innovation should adjust the predicted state estimate
The covariance of the measurement noise only
The initial conditions of the state vector
questions.explanation: The Kalman gain represents the optimal weighting between the predicted state and the measurement innovation. It balances prediction and measurement uncertainty, determining how much trust to place in the new measurement relative to the prior prediction.

questions.question: Why is the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) necessary for nonlinear systems instead of applying the standard Kalman Filter directly?
choices: Nonlinear systems have higher computational requirements
The Kalman Filter assumes linear state and measurement models; applying it directly to nonlinear systems violates optimality guarantees and can cause estimation divergence
Nonlinear systems cannot be represented with Gaussian distributions
The EKF requires fewer iterations to converge
questions.explanation: The standard Kalman Filter derives its optimality from linearity and Gaussian assumptions. When dynamics or measurements are nonlinear, propagating Gaussians through these nonlinearities produces non-Gaussian distributions. The EKF linearizes around the current estimate to approximate the nonlinear transformation while maintaining Gaussianity.

questions.question: A robot uses an EKF to estimate its position from wheel odometry (nonlinear due to heading-dependent motion) and GPS measurements. What is the primary limitation of using first-order Taylor expansion in the EKF linearization?
choices: It cannot handle GPS measurement noise
It ignores higher-order terms, introducing linearization errors that can cause filter divergence if nonlinearity is severe
It requires perfect knowledge of the system Jacobian
It is incompatible with discrete-time systems
questions.explanation: EKF linearization using first-order Taylor expansion (Jacobian matrices) neglects second and higher-order terms. When the system has strong nonlinearities or the current estimate has high uncertainty, these ignored terms can accumulate, degrading filter performance or causing divergence. Higher-order filters or particle filters can mitigate this.

questions.question: Consider a 2D Gaussian random variable with mean μ = [0, 0]ᵀ and covariance P = diag(1, 4). After applying the linear transformation y = Ax where A = [[2, 1], [0, 1]], what is the covariance of the transformed variable y?
questions.explanation: For a linear transformation y = Ax, the covariance transforms as P_y = A·P·Aᵀ. Computing: A·P·Aᵀ = [[2,1],[0,1]]·[[1,0],[0,4]]·[[2,0],[1,1]] = [[2,4],[0,4]]·[[2,0],[1,1]] = [[5,4],[4,4]]. This property is fundamental to how the Kalman Filter propagates uncertainty.

questions.question: In the Kalman Filter prediction step, the state covariance increases due to process noise Q. Which of the following scenarios would result in the largest increase in position uncertainty for an autonomous vehicle using constant-velocity motion model?
choices: High velocity with low process noise covariance
Low velocity with high process noise covariance
The process noise is independent of velocity; uncertainty increase depends only on Q magnitude and time step
Uncertainty decreases regardless of Q when velocity is nonzero
questions.explanation: In the Kalman Filter prediction step, the covariance update is P⁻ = F·P·Fᵀ + Q, where the uncertainty growth is determined by the process noise Q and the state transition Jacobian F, not by the state values themselves. The magnitude of Q directly controls how much model uncertainty is injected at each time step.

questions.question: An EKF for a wheeled robot becomes divergent when turning sharply. Which combination of modifications would best address this issue while maintaining real-time performance?
choices: Increase measurement noise covariance R and decrease process noise Q
Switch to an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) which captures nonlinearity better through weighted sigma points, or adaptively tune Q to reflect actual model uncertainty during maneuvers
Reduce the state vector dimension and ignore heading information
Increase the Kalman gain K to trust measurements more heavily
questions.explanation: Sharp turns reveal EKF limitations because the Jacobian linearization becomes inaccurate over the sharp nonlinearity. The UKF addresses this by using multiple sigma points to better capture nonlinear transformations without explicit Jacobian computation. Alternatively, adaptive Q tuning lets the filter adjust its trust in the motion model during high-curvature maneuvers. Simply increasing K can cause instability.

questions.question: In the Extended Kalman Filter, why is linearization of the nonlinear system model necessary around the current state estimate?
choices: To reduce computational complexity to O(n²) instead of O(n³)
To enable the use of linear Gaussian probability distributions in the prediction and update steps
To guarantee convergence of the filter in finite time
To eliminate the need for sensor measurements
questions.explanation: The EKF linearizes the nonlinear system using Taylor series expansion (Jacobian matrices) to maintain compatibility with linear Kalman filter equations, which assume Gaussian distributions. This approximation allows tractable estimation when the system is nearly linear around the state estimate.

questions.question: When implementing parameter estimation via EKF for Project 2, what is the key advantage of augmenting the state vector to include unknown parameters?
choices: It eliminates the need for process noise covariance
It allows simultaneous estimation of both system states and parameters using a single filter framework
It guarantees that all parameters will converge to their true values
It reduces the measurement update computational cost by half
questions.explanation: By augmenting the state vector with unknown parameters, EKF treats parameters as slowly-varying states that are updated alongside traditional states. This unified approach leverages the filter's recursive learning mechanism without requiring separate parameter estimation algorithms.

questions.question: Consider an autonomous vehicle estimating wheel slip coefficient μ in real-time using EKF. If the Jacobian matrix for the parameter dynamics becomes nearly singular, what is the primary consequence?
choices: The filter will immediately diverge and provide unrealistic estimates
The filter's observability of the parameter decreases, reducing estimation accuracy and increasing state estimate uncertainty
The measurement noise covariance matrix must be increased to compensate
The parameter will oscillate indefinitely around its true value
questions.explanation: A nearly singular Jacobian indicates poor observability—the parameter change has minimal effect on measurable outputs. This causes the filter to gain limited information from measurements, reducing its ability to distinguish between different parameter values and increasing estimation uncertainty.

questions.question: In Project 2, you need to estimate both position and a friction coefficient. Which state augmentation approach is most appropriate for EKF?
choices: Include friction as a constant-velocity model in the augmented state
Include friction as a white-noise-driven process with small process noise
Estimate friction separately using offline least-squares regression
Increase sensor sampling rate instead of augmenting the state
questions.explanation: Since friction coefficients typically vary slowly or remain relatively constant, modeling them as states with small process noise (near-constant model) allows the EKF to track gradual changes while maintaining estimation stability. This is superior to treating them as true constants, which would ignore potential variations.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the process noise covariance Q and the convergence rate of parameter estimation in an augmented-state EKF?
choices: Larger Q always results in faster parameter convergence regardless of observability
Q values for parameter states control the rate at which the filter permits parameter changes; larger Q allows faster adaptation but risks instability
Q only affects the prediction step and has no influence on parameter learning
The relationship is nonlinear and cannot be characterized analytically
questions.explanation: Tuning Q for augmented parameters is critical: high Q allows rapid parameter changes but may cause noise sensitivity and divergence, while low Q provides stability but slow convergence. The optimal choice depends on the true parameter variation rate and measurement quality.

questions.question: In your Project 2 implementation, the EKF's parameter estimates become erratic after 30 seconds despite stable sensor inputs. Which combination of issues is most likely causing this?
choices: The state estimate diverged due to incorrect initial covariance; decreasing initial P₀ will resolve this
The parameter is unobservable from available measurements and process noise Q is too large, causing filter gain to alternate between over-trusting measurements and ignoring them
The measurement noise covariance R is too small; increase R to stabilize the estimates
The nonlinear system is too complex for EKF; only linear Kalman filtering will work
questions.explanation: When parameters are unobservable (measurement residuals don't correlate with parameter changes) and Q is large, the filter permits arbitrary parameter variations while receiving insufficient correction from measurements. This creates erratic behavior as the filter cannot learn the true parameter value from available information. Observability analysis and Q tuning are necessary.

questions.question: Consider implementing EKF parameter estimation on an embedded system with 100 ms sampling time. How should you address the computational constraint of computing Jacobian matrices while maintaining estimation performance?
choices: Compute Jacobians analytically at design time and update them only when state changes significantly; validate that approximation error remains acceptable
Skip Jacobian computation entirely and use numerical differentiation which is always more stable
Increase the sampling time to 500 ms to allow sufficient computational budget
Use only the diagonal elements of the Jacobian to reduce computation; off-diagonal terms are negligible
questions.explanation: Analytical Jacobian pre-computation and selective updates (e.g., based on state magnitude changes) reduces real-time burden while maintaining accuracy if approximation error stays within acceptable bounds. This is a practical approach for embedded EKF implementation—skipping Jacobians or using incomplete calculations risks filter accuracy.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using dynamic programming over naive recursive approaches when solving the shortest path problem?
choices: It eliminates redundant computation through memoization and optimal substructure
It guarantees finding the path in linear time
It works with negative edge weights
It requires less memory allocation
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming avoids recomputing the same subproblems by storing intermediate results, which is the key distinction from naive recursion. While efficient, it doesn't guarantee linear time complexity and still cannot handle negative weights like Bellman-Ford.

questions.question: In Dijkstra's algorithm, why must all edge weights be non-negative for the algorithm to guarantee an optimal solution?
choices: Negative weights cause the algorithm to visit nodes in the wrong order
Once a node is marked as visited with the shortest distance, that distance cannot be improved by any path through unvisited nodes with non-negative weights
Negative weights create infinite loops in the priority queue
The algorithm's time complexity becomes exponential with negative weights
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach assumes that once a node is selected as having the minimum distance, no other path can improve it. This property only holds when all weights are non-negative, as adding negative edges could create shorter paths to already-processed nodes.

questions.question: Which data structure is most efficient for implementing Dijkstra's algorithm, and why?
choices: Stack, because it naturally processes nodes in reverse order
Binary heap or priority queue, because it enables O(log V) insertion and extraction of minimum distances
Adjacency matrix, because it provides O(1) edge lookup
Linked list, because it allows sequential access to all nodes
questions.explanation: A priority queue (typically implemented as a binary heap) allows efficient selection of the minimum distance node in O(log V) time. While adjacency matrices provide fast edge lookups, they don't help with the core bottleneck of finding minimum distances across potentially all remaining nodes.

questions.question: An autonomous mobile robot must navigate a grid-based environment with varying terrain costs. The robot needs to find the optimal path from start to goal minimizing energy consumption. What is the key consideration when applying Dijkstra's algorithm versus A* in this scenario?
choices: Dijkstra's algorithm is always faster regardless of heuristic availability
If a good heuristic function (admissible estimate to goal) exists, A* will explore fewer nodes than Dijkstra's by incorporating this additional guidance
Dijkstra's algorithm can handle negative terrain costs while A* cannot
A* requires the grid to be uniform while Dijkstra's works with arbitrary terrain costs
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm explores nodes based solely on their distance from the start, while A* incorporates heuristic information about proximity to the goal. When a good heuristic is available, A* prunes the search space more effectively. However, Dijkstra's is guaranteed optimal even without heuristics.

questions.question: Consider a dynamic programming solution for robot motion planning where dp[i][j] represents the minimum cost to reach cell (i,j). If a cell is blocked, how should this be handled in the recurrence relation?
choices: Set dp[i][j] = 0 to ignore blocked cells
Set dp[i][j] = infinity or an invalid marker to prevent paths through blocked cells
Skip updating dp[i][j] and treat it as unreachable
Set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] with a penalty factor
questions.explanation: Blocked cells should be marked with infinity (or a sentinel value representing impossibility) to ensure that any path attempting to use them will have infinite cost, effectively preventing their selection in optimal solutions. This maintains the correctness of the dynamic programming approach.

questions.question: An autonomous vehicle uses Dijkstra's algorithm on a road network represented as a weighted directed graph where edge weights represent travel time. If the vehicle discovers during execution that a previously traversed edge now has a lower weight (due to traffic changes), how would you efficiently update the shortest paths?
choices: Re-run Dijkstra's algorithm from scratch on the entire graph
Use a dynamic shortest path algorithm like D* or D* Lite that incrementally updates affected paths without recomputing from scratch
Update only the affected nodes by running Dijkstra's from those nodes
Apply the Bellman-Ford algorithm as a one-time correction step
questions.explanation: When the environment changes dynamically (as in real autonomous systems), algorithms like D* and D* Lite are designed to incrementally propagate changes to affected paths efficiently. Re-running Dijkstra's from scratch is inefficient for frequent updates, making specialized dynamic algorithms superior for real-time systems.

questions.question: In a multi-robot autonomous system, each robot uses dynamic programming to compute collision-free paths. Why is decomposing the global path-planning problem into independent DP subproblems for each robot potentially suboptimal, and what alternative approach might address this?
choices: Because robots may interfere with each other's paths; using centralized planning or coordination mechanisms ensures global optimality
Because dynamic programming cannot handle multiple robots regardless of coordination strategy
Because independent DP solutions guarantee local but not global optimality; however, sequential or cooperative planning with conflict resolution can improve coordination
Because Dijkstra's algorithm is incompatible with multi-agent scenarios
questions.explanation: When each robot independently computes an optimal path using DP, they may not account for interactions with other robots, leading to suboptimal global solutions or even conflicts. Sequential planning (planning robots one-by-one with awareness of previous paths) or cooperative approaches with negotiation improve coordination while maintaining computational tractability compared to fully centralized planning.

questions.question: In EKF-SLAM, what is the primary purpose of the prediction step in the Kalman filter cycle?
choices: To estimate the robot's new pose and map state based on motion model and previous estimates
To update the covariance matrix using landmark observations
To correct measurement errors in the sensor data
To initialize new landmarks in the feature map
questions.explanation: The prediction step uses the motion model to propagate the state estimate forward in time, predicting where the robot and landmarks should be before incorporating new measurements. This is fundamental to the Kalman filter's recursive structure.

questions.question: Why is the loop closure detection problem particularly challenging in visual SLAM systems?
choices: It requires real-time processing of high-resolution images
Viewpoint changes, lighting variations, and dynamic environments can make recognizing previously visited locations difficult
It depends entirely on GPS availability
The computational cost of feature matching is negligible compared to other SLAM components
questions.explanation: Loop closure detection must handle perceptual aliasing where different locations appear similar or the same location appears different due to environmental changes. This makes robust place recognition a critical and challenging component of visual SLAM systems.

questions.question: In a deep reinforcement learning agent learning to navigate an autonomous mobile robot, what is the relationship between the exploration-exploitation trade-off and convergence speed?
choices: Higher exploration always leads to faster convergence regardless of the environment
Pure exploitation (no exploration) guarantees optimal policy learning in finite time
Insufficient exploration may trap the agent in local optima, while excessive exploration delays convergence; optimal balance is problem-dependent
Exploration and exploitation are independent parameters that do not affect each other
questions.explanation: The exploration-exploitation trade-off is fundamental to RL: too little exploration may cause the agent to converge to suboptimal policies, while too much exploration wastes time sampling low-value actions. Finding the optimal balance depends on the specific problem structure and available computational resources.

questions.question: Consider an MPC controller for an autonomous vehicle with a prediction horizon of 10 steps and a 100 ms sampling time. What is a primary advantage of MPC for this application compared to classical PID control?
choices: MPC has lower computational requirements than PID controllers
MPC can explicitly handle multi-step constraints and optimize over a future trajectory, incorporating both state and input constraints
MPC does not require a vehicle dynamics model
PID controllers are impossible to implement in real-time systems
questions.explanation: MPC's key advantage is its ability to predict future states over a horizon and optimize a cost function while respecting constraints like steering angle limits and collision avoidance. This makes it superior to PID for constrained trajectory tracking problems.

questions.question: A SLAM system using particle filters maintains N particles representing hypotheses about the robot's pose and map. As the robot moves through an environment with increasing uncertainty, the particle filter begins to suffer from particle degeneracy. Which technique most effectively addresses this issue?
choices: Increasing the sampling frequency of sensor measurements
Resampling particles proportionally to their importance weights, removing low-probability hypotheses and duplicating high-probability ones
Decreasing the number of particles to reduce computational load
Removing all observations that have measurement noise above a threshold
questions.explanation: Particle degeneracy occurs when most particles have negligible weight. Resampling (multinomial or importance resampling) is the standard solution that removes unlikely particles and concentrates computation on promising hypotheses, maintaining effective sample size in the filter.

questions.question: In policy gradient reinforcement learning methods like REINFORCE or Actor-Critic algorithms, explain why using a baseline function (such as a value function estimate) in the gradient computation reduces variance without introducing bias in the policy gradient estimator. What mathematical property enables this?
choices: The baseline must be independent of the action taken, and the expected value of the baseline times the gradient of log-probability is zero
The baseline function is always set to zero in unbiased implementations
Baselines introduce positive bias that exactly cancels negative bias from policy gradients
The variance reduction property only holds for deterministic policies, not stochastic ones
questions.explanation: A baseline b(s) that depends only on state (not action) satisfies E[∇log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0, so subtracting it from the advantage does not change the gradient's expectation (remains unbiased) but reduces variance. This is because ∇log π(a|s) is the score function, and the baseline is independent of action sampling.

questions.question: For a nonlinear MPC controlling a robot manipulator with 6 DOF, the controller must solve a nonconvex optimization problem at each sampling instant. Which combination of strategies would best balance performance, constraint satisfaction, and real-time feasibility?
choices: Use a global optimization method like simulated annealing for guaranteed optimality at each step
Implement successive linearization (DDP or iLQR) around nominal trajectories with warm-starting from previous solutions, combined with constraint tightening for robustness
Simplify to linear MPC by ignoring nonlinear dynamics to guarantee fast computation
Increase the sampling time to 10 seconds to allow sufficient computation between control updates
questions.explanation: Successive linearization methods like DDP/iLQR provide fast local optimization suitable for real-time control. Warm-starting leverages previous solutions to reduce computation. Constraint tightening provides robustness margins to account for linearization errors and disturbances, balancing the three requirements effectively.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the primary advantage of a closed-loop control system over an open-loop system?
choices: Closed-loop systems automatically correct for disturbances and errors by measuring the output and adjusting the input
Closed-loop systems are always cheaper and simpler to implement than open-loop systems
Closed-loop systems eliminate the need for any mathematical modeling of the plant
Closed-loop systems can operate without any sensors or measurement devices
questions.explanation: Closed-loop systems use feedback to continuously monitor output and adjust inputs to minimize error, making them robust to disturbances. Open-loop systems cannot respond to unexpected changes because they do not measure the actual output.

questions.question: In a closed-loop feedback system, what is the role of the error signal?
choices: To measure the temperature of the system components
To represent the difference between the desired setpoint and the actual measured output, driving corrective action
To amplify the input signal before it reaches the plant
To store historical data about system performance
questions.explanation: The error signal (e = setpoint - measured output) is the foundation of feedback control. It tells the controller how much adjustment is needed to bring the system to the desired state.

questions.question: Consider a cruise control system in a car. If the car encounters a hill and starts to slow down, how does a closed-loop feedback system respond compared to an open-loop system?
choices: Both systems would respond identically by increasing engine power automatically
The open-loop system would maintain constant throttle (no response), while the closed-loop system would increase throttle based on detected speed loss
The closed-loop system would disable the engine to save fuel, while open-loop would accelerate
Neither system can respond to hills because they are external disturbances
questions.explanation: An open-loop cruise control applies fixed throttle regardless of disturbances, so the car would slow down on a hill. A closed-loop system measures actual speed, detects the error, and increases throttle to maintain the setpoint speed.

questions.question: Which statement about feedback in control systems is incorrect?
choices: Negative feedback reduces the error between setpoint and output
Positive feedback amplifies the error and can lead to system instability
Feedback requires measurement of the controlled variable through sensors
Feedback always guarantees that the system will reach steady-state without oscillation
questions.explanation: While feedback improves control performance, it does not guarantee stable operation. A poorly designed closed-loop system with excessive gain can oscillate or become unstable. Stability must be specifically analyzed and designed for.

questions.question: A manufacturing process uses an open-loop control system to maintain oven temperature by setting a fixed power level. What is a significant limitation of this approach?
choices: The system cannot operate without continuous human monitoring
It cannot compensate for changes in ambient temperature, thermal losses, or variations in load, causing temperature drift
It requires more expensive components than a closed-loop system
It is impossible to achieve the desired temperature with an open-loop system
questions.explanation: Open-loop systems apply a predetermined input without measuring output. If external conditions change (e.g., room temperature drops, thermal insulation degrades), the oven temperature will drift because there is no feedback to detect and correct for these disturbances.

questions.question: In designing a feedback control system for a robotic arm position, which of the following components is NOT essential?
choices: A sensor to measure the actual arm position
A controller that computes the error and determines corrective action
A motor or actuator to move the arm toward the desired position
A wireless communication system to send setpoint commands from a smartphone
questions.explanation: While wireless communication may be convenient, it is not essential for basic feedback control. The core components are: sensor (feedback), controller (decision logic), and actuator (corrective action). The setpoint can be hardcoded, manually set, or transmitted by various means without affecting control system fundamentals.

questions.question: A water heater maintains temperature using a thermostat that turns the heating element on when temperature drops below 60°C and off when it reaches 65°C. Analyze this system: what type of control strategy is this, and what could be improved?
choices: This is a proportional control system; it could be improved by adding derivative terms to reduce oscillation
This is a bang-bang (on-off) closed-loop control system; it could be improved by using proportional control to reduce temperature overshoot and oscillation around the setpoint
This is an open-loop system; it cannot maintain temperature without continuous manual adjustment
This is optimal control and no improvement is possible without adding more expensive sensors
questions.explanation: The thermostat uses on-off feedback control (bang-bang), which is simple but causes temperature oscillation between 60-65°C. Proportional control would modulate heat input continuously based on error magnitude, reducing oscillations and improving comfort and energy efficiency.

questions.question: A mass-spring-damper system is described by the differential equation: m(d²x/dt²) + c(dx/dt) + kx = F(t). What is the order of this system?
choices: First-order
